WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.clue_en: In 1851, this chief minister founded the Dar al-Fonun polytechnic in Tehran before being dismissed and executed in the Fin Garden bathhouse of Kashan.
WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.expl_en: Mirza Taqi Khan Amir Kabir founded the Dar al-Fonun in 1851 to train military officers, doctors, and engineers in modern sciences, but court rivalries led Nasir al-Din Shah to order his execution in Fin Garden in January 1852.

WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.clue_en: Following the defeat in the Second Russo-Persian War, Crown Prince Abbas Mirza negotiated this 1828 treaty, ceding Erivan and Nakhchivan to the Russian Empire and establishing the Aras River as the border.
WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.expl_en: The 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay ended the second war with Russia, imposing humiliating extraterritorial capitulations and ceding all remaining Transcaucasian territories south to the Aras River.

WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.clue_en: Reigning for nearly half a century from 1848 until his assassination in 1896, this Qajar monarch became the first Iranian sovereign to tour Europe and was an avid pioneer of photography.
WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.expl_en: Nasir al-Din Shah ruled for 48 years, embarked on three grand European tours (1873, 1878, 1889), documented his court with personal photography, and was assassinated by Mirza Reza Kermani in 1896.

WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.clue_en: In December 1891, Grand Ayatollah Mirza Hasan Shirazi issued a telegram from Samarra forbidding the consumption of this commodity as war against the Hidden Imam, forcing the cancellation of a British imperial concession.
WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.expl_en: The 1891–1892 Tobacco Protest united merchants, intellectuals, and clergy against Major Talbot's monopoly, demonstrating for the first time that mass civil disobedience could overturn imperial concessions.

WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.clue_en: Born to an Armenian family in New Julfa and later serving as envoy to London, this 19th-century modernist founded the secret society Faramoushkhaneh and published the dissident reformist newspaper Qanun.
WE DON'T COTTON TO CONCESSIONS.expl_en: Mirza Malkom Khan was an influential Iranian diplomat who introduced Masonic-style secret organizing to Iran through Faramoushkhaneh in 1858 and later attacked Qajar tyranny through his London-based journal Qanun (Law).

A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.clue_en: In his contemporary account of the revolution, British scholar E.G. Browne hailed this fighter who commanded the defense of the Amirkhiz district during the 1908–1909 Royalist siege of Tabriz, earning the title Sardar-e Melli.
A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.expl_en: Sattar Khan became a legendary national hero when he refused Russian protection and rallied Tabriz fighters against Royalist besiegers, declaring he wanted all seven nations to fly the Iranian flag.

A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.clue_en: Browne recorded that in July 1906, over twelve thousand protesters took sanctuary (bast) on the garden grounds of this diplomatic mission in Tehran, refusing to leave until the Shah signed the decree granting a Constitution.
A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.expl_en: In July 1906, thousands of guild members, students, and merchants pitched tents in the British Legation gardens, utilizing British diplomatic immunity to demand a Majles and constitutional monarchy from Mozaffar al-Din Shah.

A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.clue_en: Browne documented the fierce ideological opposition led by this senior mujtahid, who broke with pro-constitution clerics to demand Mashru'eh (governance strictly under Islamic law) before being hanged in Tupkhaneh Square in 1909.
A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.expl_en: Sheikh Fazlollah Nuri argued that human legislation in parliament infringed upon divine sharia law; after the revolutionary retaking of Tehran in July 1909, he was tried for treason and hanged in public.

A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.clue_en: According to Browne's dispatches, on June 23, 1908, Mohammad Ali Shah ordered the Persian Cossack Brigade under this Russian colonel to bombard the Baharestan building housing the First Majles.
A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.expl_en: Colonel Vladimir Liakhov led the Cossack Brigade in shelling the parliament building, killing defenders, arresting deputies, and initiating the Little Autocracy (Estebdad-e Saghir).

A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.clue_en: Browne lamented the execution of Mirza Jahangir Khan, co-founder of this radical weekly satirical journal whose famed columnist Ali-Akbar Dehkhoda penned the biting satirical column Charand-o Parand.
A MASH-RUTEH MADE IN HEAVEN.expl_en: Sur-e Esrafil (Trumpet of Gabriel) was the most popular and influential journal of the revolution; after the 1908 coup, Jahangir Khan was strangled in Bagh-e Shah, prompting Dehkhoda's immortal elegy 'Yad Ar, Ze Sham-e Morde, Yad Ar'.

OIL, OBVIOUSLY.clue_en: In The Coup, Ervand Abrahamian details how on May 1, 1951, this newly appointed prime minister signed into law the nationalization of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, triggering a global British boycott.
OIL, OBVIOUSLY.expl_en: Dr. Mohammad Mosaddegh led the National Front to pass the oil nationalization bill through the Majles and Senate in April 1951, becoming Prime Minister to implement the expulsion of the British AIOC from Khuzestan.

OIL, OBVIOUSLY.clue_en: Abrahamian identifies this grandson of Theodore Roosevelt and CIA Near East chief as the field officer who slipped into Tehran in July 1953 to coordinate the coup against Mosaddegh.
OIL, OBVIOUSLY.expl_en: Kermit Roosevelt Jr. directed Operation TPAJAX on the ground in Tehran, operating from safe houses to orchestrate street mobs, military units under General Zahedi, and bribed journalists.

OIL, OBVIOUSLY.clue_en: While the American CIA operation in August 1953 was codenamed TPAJAX, Abrahamian notes that the British Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) carried out their parallel plan under this codename.
OIL, OBVIOUSLY.expl_en: The British SIS/MI6 operation was originally codenamed Operation Boot, conceived under Anthony Eden and Winston Churchill before being merged with the American CIA's TPAJAX.

OIL, OBVIOUSLY.clue_en: Abrahamian recounts the fate of Mosaddegh's 34-year-old foreign minister, editor of Bakhtar-e Emruz, who went into hiding after the 1953 coup but was captured, stabbed, and executed by firing squad in November 1954.
OIL, OBVIOUSLY.expl_en: Dr. Hossein Fatemi was Mosaddegh's closest and most outspoken republican lieutenant; the post-coup military regime singled him out for execution after he delivered fiery speeches attacking the royal dynasty.

OIL, OBVIOUSLY.clue_en: Abrahamian demonstrates that the coup culminated in October 1954 with a 25-year consortium agreement with Western majors, in which the former British monopolist (AIOC) retained this specific percentage share.
OIL, OBVIOUSLY.expl_en: Under the 1954 Consortium Agreement negotiated by Herbert Hoover Jr. and Ali Amini, British Petroleum retained 40%, five US oil companies took 40%, Royal Dutch Shell received 14%, and CFP of France received 6%.

DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.ans_en: The 2,500-Year Celebration of the Persian Empire
DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.clue_en: In his court diary, Asadollah Alam recorded frantic logistical preparations for this lavish October 1971 gala among ancient ruins, featuring catering flown in from Maxim's de Paris for foreign monarchs and heads of state.
opts_en: The 2,500-Year Celebration of the Persian Empire
DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.expl_en: The 2,500-year celebration of the Persian Empire in October 1971 brought dozens of world leaders to a luxury tent city in Persepolis, which critics lambasted for extravagant excess while ordinary villages lacked water.

DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.clue_en: In May 1972, Alam noted in his diary the high-stakes Tehran visit of this US President, during which the White House granted the Shah an unprecedented 'blank check' to purchase any non-nuclear American military hardware.
DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.expl_en: Richard Nixon and Henry Kissinger stopped in Tehran in May 1972 returning from Moscow, agreeing that Iran would act as the primary regional military protector of the Persian Gulf under the Nixon Doctrine.

DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.clue_en: Throughout his court diaries, Alam repeatedly vented his contempt for this rival statesman, who served as Iran's longest-tenured prime minister for twelve years from 1965 to 1977 before being scapegoated and arrested in 1978.
DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.expl_en: Amir Abbas Hoveyda, known for his signature pipe and orchid boutonnière, ran the civilian bureaucracy for twelve years, but Alam continually accused him in his diaries of subservience and fiscal corruption.

DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.clue_en: Alam noted with quiet dread in March 1975 that the Shah abruptly dissolved Iran's existing political parties and established this single totalitarian state party, telling dissidents to take their passports and leave.
DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.expl_en: The Hezb-e Rastakhiz (Resurgence Party) established monolithic one-party rule, forcing all civil servants and citizens to enroll, alienating the traditional bazaar through heavy-handed price controls.

DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.clue_en: In March 1975, Alam recorded the Shah's triumphant mood following the signing of an accord in Algiers with Saddam Hussein, which delimited the border along the thalweg of this disputed river waterway in exchange for cutting off aid to Iraqi Kurds.
DEAR DIARY: THE SHAH SPEAKS.expl_en: The 1975 Algiers Agreement secured Iranian sovereignty over half the Arvand Rud/Shatt al-Arab along the median channel (thalweg), but five years later Saddam Hussein tore up the agreement on Iraqi television to launch the 1980 invasion.

WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.clue_en: In his 1970 lecture series delivered in exile in Najaf, published in Islam and Revolution, Ayatollah Khomeini set forth this foundational constitutional doctrine, asserting that qualified Islamic jurists possess the divine mandate to govern.
WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.expl_en: In Hukumat-e Islami: Velayat-e Faqih, Khomeini revolutionized Shi'i jurisprudence by arguing that political governance is not meant to remain dormant during the occultation of the Twelfth Imam, but must be exercised by the just faqih.

WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.clue_en: In a fiery October 1964 sermon in Qom that led directly to his exile, Khomeini denounced the Majles for granting judicial immunity to military personnel from this foreign nation, declaring: 'They have sold our independence!'
WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.expl_en: Khomeini's October 26, 1964 speech denounced the Status of Forces Agreement granting diplomatic immunity to American military advisers and their dependents, leading the Shah to arrest and deport him to Turkey on November 4.

WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.clue_en: After being moved from Turkey in 1965, Khomeini lived for thirteen years in this Iraqi holy shrine city, developing his revolutionary political treatises until Saddam Hussein forced him out in autumn 1978.
WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.expl_en: Khomeini taught at the Sheikh Ansari Mosque in Najaf from October 1965 until October 1978, when the Ba'athist government pressured him to leave, prompting his brief fateful relocation to Neauphle-le-Château outside Paris.

WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.clue_en: In Islam and Revolution, Khomeini systematically applied this Quranic term—originally denoting an idol, false deity, or tyrant who oversteps divine limits—to brand the Pahlavi monarchy as illegitimate.
WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.expl_en: Khomeini categorized the monarchy as a Taghuti regime, maintaining that obedience to any ruler not governing by divine law constitutes worship of a false idol.

WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.clue_en: In his declarations from 1963, Khomeini condemned the violent assault carried out by Pahlavi paratroopers on March 22, 1963—the martyrdom anniversary of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq—against students inside this venerable Qom seminary.
WHAT KHOMEINI ACTUALLY SAID.expl_en: The assault on the Fayziyeh seminary in Qom in March 1963 killed several talabehs (seminary students) and outraged the religious establishment, directly setting the stage for the June 1963 (15 Khordad) uprisings.

LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.clue_en: In A Social History of Iranian Cinema, Hamid Naficy credits this royal court photographer, who accompanied Mozaffar al-Din Shah to the 1900 Paris Exposition, with purchasing a Gaumont camera and shooting the earliest motion pictures of Iran.
LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.expl_en: Mirza Ebrahim Khan Akkas-bashi filmed Mozaffar al-Din Shah inspecting the festival of flowers in Ostend, Belgium in August 1900, marking the inception of Iranian cinematography.

LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.clue_en: Naficy chronicles the historic debut of this 1933 film—directed by Ardeshir Irani and Abdolhossein Sepanta at the Imperial Film Company in Bombay—which premiered in Tehran as the very first sound film in the Persian language.
LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.expl_en: Dokhtar-e Lor (The Lor Girl, subtitled 'The Iran of Yesterday and the Iran of Today') captivated audiences with synchronized sound, dialogue, and Persian music recorded in India.

LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.clue_en: Playing the heroine Golnar in the 1933 film The Lor Girl, this pioneering performer made history as the first Iranian woman to ever appear unveiled on a motion picture screen, enduring severe social ostracism upon returning to Iran.
LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.expl_en: Sedigheh (Roohangiz) Saminejad, the wife of an Imperial Film Company employee in Bombay, took on the historic role of Golnar; the backlash from conservative society was so severe she lived the rest of her life in seclusion.

LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.clue_en: Naficy details how this Armenian-Iranian filmmaker, who studied at the Cinema Academy of Moscow, established Iran's first film training school in 1930 and directed the first Iranian silent feature film, Abi and Rabi.
LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.expl_en: Ovanes Ohanian founded the Parvareshgah-e Artisti-ye Sinama (Cinema Artist School) in Tehran in 1930 and directed the comedy *Abi and Rabi*, starring himself and Mohammad Zarrabi in tall-and-short comedy routines.

LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.clue_en: Founded in the late 1920s on Lalezar Street inside a famed luxury hotel by merchant Ali Vakili, this venue was the premier cinema palace of interwar Tehran, introducing orchestral overtures and dedicated family screenings.
LIGHTS ON LALEZAR.expl_en: The Grand Cinema, situated inside the Grand Hotel on Lalezar Street, played a vital role in popularizing bourgeois cinema attendance, complete with a Western-style buffet, printed synopses, and women-only afternoons.

THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.clue_en: On February 21, 1921, this Cossack brigade colonel marched his troops from Qazvin to seize Tehran, launching his ascent to the throne as the founder of the Pahlavi dynasty.
THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.expl_en: Reza Khan led 3,000 Cossacks into Tehran in February 1921, becoming commander-in-chief (Sardar-e Sepah), prime minister in 1923, and Shah in 1925.

THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.clue_en: Completed in 1938 without any foreign borrowing by taxing sugar and tea, this 1,394-kilometer engineering marvel connected the Caspian Sea to the Persian Gulf.
THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.expl_en: Inaugurated in August 1938, it conquered the Alborz and Zagros mountains with 4,100 bridges and 224 tunnels entirely funded through domestic monopolies on sugar and tea.

THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.clue_en: Founded in 1934 under Minister of Education Ali-Asghar Hekmat, this institution became Iran's premier modern university, whose master plan was drawn by French architect André Godard.
THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.expl_en: Established by the Majles in 1934, the University of Tehran consolidated medicine, law, literature, and engineering into a single secular academy.

THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.clue_en: In January 1936, following a state visit to Atatürk's Turkey, Reza Shah issued the controversial royal decree known by this Persian name, enforcing the unveiling of women.
THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.expl_en: Decreed on January 7, 1936, Kashf-e Hejab mandated that women appear unveiled in public and required police to confiscate traditional headcoverings.

THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.clue_en: Wielding immense power as Minister of Court until his fall from favor during the 1932 oil negotiations, this statesman was assassinated in Qasr Prison in 1933.
THE IRON COSSACK: REZA SHAH.expl_en: Teymourtash was widely viewed as the second most powerful man in Iran; accused of bribery and Russian connections, he was murdered by prison physician Dr. Ahmadi.

ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.clue_en: Moving the Safavid capital from Qazvin to Isfahan in 1598, this fifth monarch laid out Naqsh-e Jahan Square and transformed Iran into a commercial superpower.
ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.expl_en: Shah Abbas I (r. 1587–1629) centralized Safavid authority, created the royal workshops, and built Isfahan into 'Nesf-e Jahan' (Half the World).

ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.clue_en: To dominate the global raw silk market, Shah Abbas resettled thousands of Christian Armenian merchants on the south bank of the Zayandeh River in this Isfahan suburb.
ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.expl_en: Founded in 1604, New Julfa was granted religious freedom and a monopoly on the silk export trade, funding majestic churches like Vank Cathedral.

ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.clue_en: Constructed on the eastern flank of Naqsh-e Jahan for the royal court, this private mosque features no minarets or courtyard and is renowned for its shifting cream-to-pink dome.
ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.expl_en: Completed in 1619 by master builder Mohammad Reza Isfahani, Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque was connected to the Ali Qapu palace via a subterranean passage under the square.

ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.clue_en: Wearing distinctive scarlet 12-gored turbans honoring the Twelve Imams, these Turkmen tribal warriors formed the fanatic shock troops that established the Safavid state.
ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.expl_en: The Qizilbash ('Red Heads') were tribal devotees of the Safaviyya Sufi order who revered the early Safavid shahs as both king and spiritual master (Murshid-e Kamel).

ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.clue_en: In August 1514, Ottoman Sultan Selim I deployed massed field artillery and musketeers to shatter Shah Ismail's cavalry at this fateful northwestern battlefield.
ISFAHAN-TASTIC SAFFAVIDS.expl_en: The Battle of Chaldoran demonstrated the decisive superiority of Ottoman firearms over Safavid cavalry, prompting the Safavids to later modernize their army with European assistance.

NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.clue_en: In February 1739, Nader Shah shattered the vast army of Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah in just three hours at this battle north of Delhi, capturing the Peacock Throne.
NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.expl_en: At Karnal, Nader Shah used swivel guns (zamburak) on camel backs to rout the Mughal war elephants, looting Delhi of the Koh-i-Noor diamond and Peacock Throne.

NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.clue_en: Along with the Daria-i-Noor ('Sea of Light'), Nader Shah carried away from Delhi this 105-carat diamond, whose Persian name translates to 'Mountain of Light'.
NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.expl_en: Legend recounts that Nader Shah discovered the Koh-i-Noor concealed inside the Mughal Emperor's turban during a ceremonial turban-exchange ritual.

NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.clue_en: Ruling Iran from Shiraz following the chaos of Nader Shah's demise, this benevolent Zand chieftain refused the royal title of Shah, instead styling himself Vakil al-Ro'aya.
NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.expl_en: Karim Khan ruled as 'Advocate of the People' (Vakil al-Ro'aya) from 1751 to 1779, beautifying Shiraz with the Arg, Vakil Bazaar, and Vakil Mosque.

NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.clue_en: In March 1736, Nader invited over twenty thousand grandees, tribal khans, and clerics to this windswept plain in Azerbaijan to extract an ultimatum crowning him Shah.
NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.expl_en: At the grand assembly of Mughan (Quriltai), Nader demanded that Iranians renounce extreme anti-Sunni Shi'i curses (Sabb and Rafd) as a condition of his accepting the crown.

NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.clue_en: In 1794, the last courageous Zand ruler was betrayed at this desert city, blinded, and killed by Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, who ordered twenty thousand pairs of eyes gouged out.
NADER SHAH'S SWORDPLAY.expl_en: Lotf Ali Khan Zand made his final stand in Kerman; when the city fell after a six-month siege, Agha Mohammad Khan exacted monstrous vengeance, ordering mounds of eyes to be weighed before him.

OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.clue_en: Approved by President Eisenhower and Prime Minister Churchill, this official CIA alphanumeric codename designated the joint covert operation to topple Dr. Mosaddegh.
OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.expl_en: In CIA cryptographic naming, 'TP' was the country digraph for Iran, and 'AJAX' referred to the Greek mythological warrior or the household cleanser scourer.

OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.clue_en: On August 19, 1953, the CIA deployed paid street mobs and zurkhaneh musclemen led by this notorious South Tehran gang boss nicknamed 'the Brainless'.
OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.expl_en: Shaban Jafari was sprung from jail on August 19 to mobilize club-wielding thugs, wrestlers, and prostitutes from the Shahr-e Now district to ransack pro-Mosaddegh newspaper offices.

OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.clue_en: When the initial coup attempt collapsed on August 16, Mohammad Reza Shah and Queen Soraya fled the country in a personal plane, first to Baghdad and then to this European capital.
OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.expl_en: The Shah checked into the Hotel Excelsior in Rome; Allen Dulles, director of the CIA, coincidentally checked into the same hotel during his European holiday to coordinate with him.

OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.clue_en: To manufacture a veneer of legality, CIA operative Kermit Roosevelt procured signed imperial royal decrees (firmans) dismissing Mosaddegh and appointing this retired general as Prime Minister.
OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.expl_en: General Fazlollah Zahedi went into hiding at a CIA safehouse in Shemiran while the firmans were duplicated and distributed to the press to spark public unrest.

OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.clue_en: After enduring a military show trial and three years in solitary confinement, Dr. Mosaddegh was sentenced to house arrest for the rest of his life at his family estate in this village.
OPERATION AJAX & CLEANSER.expl_en: Mosaddegh was confined to Ahmadabad from 1956 until his death from cancer in March 1967; the Shah refused his request to be buried in the cemetery of martyrs of 30 Tir, burying him in his dining room.

DEFENSE OF THE REALM.clue_en: Captured by Iraqi forces after a ferocious 34-day battle in 1980, this vital port city on the Arvand Rud was triumphantly liberated on May 24, 1982, in Operation Beit ol-Moqaddas.
DEFENSE OF THE REALM.expl_en: The liberation of Khorramshahr captured 19,000 Iraqi soldiers and was hailed nationwide with the famous phrase: 'Khorramshahr was liberated by God.'

DEFENSE OF THE REALM.clue_en: Popularized by southern vocalist Gholam Koveitipour following the death of commander Mohammad Jahanara, this sorrowful Dashti elegy opens: 'Yaran cheh gharibaneh...'
DEFENSE OF THE REALM.expl_en: Gholam Koveitipour's 'Gharibaneh' became the emotional anthem of the war generation, commemorating fallen youth and commanders who never saw Khorramshahr freed.

DEFENSE OF THE REALM.clue_en: In July 1988, Ayatollah Khomeini compared accepting this United Nations Security Council ceasefire resolution to 'drinking the poisoned chalice'.
DEFENSE OF THE REALM.expl_en: Resolution 598 called for an immediate ceasefire, withdrawal of forces to international boundaries, and a commission to determine the aggressor responsible for the war.

DEFENSE OF THE REALM.clue_en: Founded by decree in November 1979 as the 'Army of Twenty Million', this volunteer auxiliary corps mobilized teenagers and elders into mass human-wave assaults.
DEFENSE OF THE REALM.expl_en: The Basij-e Mostaz'afin (Mobilization of the Oppressed) provided hundreds of thousands of volunteers wearing red forehead headbands and symbolic plastic keys to paradise.

DEFENSE OF THE REALM.clue_en: In March 1988, Saddam Hussein deployed mustard gas and sarin against this Iraqi Kurdish town following its capture by Iranian forces and peshmerga, killing over 5,000 civilians.
DEFENSE OF THE REALM.expl_en: The chemical massacre at Halabja on March 16, 1988, was documented by Iranian photojournalists like Kaveh Golestan, horrifying the global public with images of gassed families.

ZAND OF HOPE & GLORY.clue_en: Upon securing dominion over Iran in 1751, Karim Khan Zand famously refused the imperial title of Shahanshah, choosing instead this humble Arabic title meaning 'Advocate of the People'.
ZAND OF HOPE & GLORY.expl_en: Karim Khan argued that only the absent Safavid line possessed divine right, so he governed as trustee and legal advocate for the realm's subjects.

FATEMI'S LAST STAND.clue_en: Before facing the military firing squad at dawn on November 10, 1954, for his republican defiance during the 1953 coup, this 37-year-old Foreign Minister cried: 'Long live Iran! Long live Mosaddeq!'
FATEMI'S LAST STAND.expl_en: Dr. Hossein Fatemi was editor of Bakhtar-e Emruz and the architect of oil nationalization; he was the only member of Mosaddegh's cabinet executed by the Pahlavi military tribunal.

KHORRAMSHAHR UNBOUND.clue_en: Following the victorious 1982 liberation of Khorramshahr from Iraqi occupation, Ayatollah Khomeini proclaimed this famous six-word theological statement in Persian.
opts_en: The road to Jerusalem passes through Karbala
We have resisted to the end
KHORRAMSHAHR UNBOUND.expl_en: Khomeini famously sought to prevent military triumphalism and hubris by attributing the impossible victory exclusively to divine will: 'خرمشهر را خدا آزاد کرد'.

MOZAFFAR'S DYING STAMP.clue_en: Critically ill and dying only five days later on January 8, 1907, this Qajar monarch affixed his trembling signature to Iran's historic first Fundamental Law.
MOZAFFAR'S DYING STAMP.expl_en: Mozaffar al-Din Shah signed the 51 articles of the Fundamental Law on December 30, 1906, on his deathbed, establishing constitutional monarchy in Iran.

FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.clue_en: Riding his faithful stallion Rakhsh and clad in tiger-skin armor (Babr-e Bayan), this legendary champion of Zabulistan is the ultimate hero of the Shahnameh.
FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.expl_en: Rostam son of Zal is the central figure of Ferdowsi's epic, defending the Iranian crown through seven heroic trials (Haft Khan).

FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.clue_en: Nesting upon Mount Damavand, this benevolent mythical giant bird fostered the albino child Zal and later advised Rostam on how to overcome the invulnerable Esfandiyar.
FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.expl_en: The Simurgh represents divine wisdom in Iranian mythology, famously reappearing in Attar of Nishapur's mystical Conference of the Birds.

FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.clue_en: Seduced by Ahriman who kissed his shoulders, this tyrannical serpent-king sprouted two ravenous serpents that had to be fed the brains of young Iranian men daily.
FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.expl_en: Zahhak's thousand-year reign of terror was ended when the blacksmith Kaveh raised his leather apron as a banner of revolt, helping Prince Fereydun chain Zahhak inside Mount Damavand.

FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.clue_en: After eighteen of his sons were slaughtered to feed Zahhak's serpents, this Isfahani blacksmith hoisted his leather apron on a spear, creating the imperial standard Derafsh Kaviani.
FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.expl_en: Kaveh's apron was embellished with jewels and gold by successive kings to become Derafsh-e Kaviani, the sacred royal banner of pre-Islamic Iran until the Arab conquest.

FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.clue_en: Falsely accused of seducing his stepmother Sudabeh, this paragon of virtue proved his innocence by riding through a mountain of roaring fire unburned.
FERDOWSI'S RHYME TIME.expl_en: Siavash was later unjustly murdered in Turan by king Afrasiyab; from his spilled blood grew the crimson flower known as 'Blood of Siavash' (Khoon-e Siavashan), inaugurating annual rites of national mourning.

BAZAAR-O WORLD.clue_en: In December 1905, the public bastinado (foot-whipping) of two respected sugar merchants ordered by Governor Ala al-Dowleh sparked the uprising that led to this national revolution.
BAZAAR-O WORLD.expl_en: When sugar prices spiked due to the Russo-Japanese War, Governor Ala al-Dowleh beat elderly merchant Seyyed Hashem Qandi, prompting merchants and clerics to shut the Grand Bazaar and take sanctuary (bast) at Shah Abdol-Azim.

BAZAAR-O WORLD.clue_en: Renowned for its fine silk weaves, floral Shah Abbasi arabesques, and master weavers like Seirafian, this central city's carpets are world-famous alongside Tabriz and Kashan.
BAZAAR-O WORLD.expl_en: Isfahan's carpet workshops date back to the royal Safavid ateliers of the 16th century, famed for asymmetrical knots, silk foundations, and balanced central medallions.

BAZAAR-O WORLD.clue_en: Producing over ninety percent of the world's supply of this 'red gold', the arid southern plains of this northeastern province are the global center of crocus cultivation.
BAZAAR-O WORLD.expl_en: Cities like Qaen and Torbat-e Heydariyeh in Khorasan yield the world's most prized Sargol and Negin saffron threads.

BAZAAR-O WORLD.clue_en: In May 1901, Mozaffar al-Din Shah granted this British socialite and investor a sixty-year concession covering three-quarters of Iran to search for oil in exchange for £20,000 cash.
BAZAAR-O WORLD.expl_en: D'Arcy nearly went bankrupt drilling in the scorching heat of Khuzestan until striking oil at Masjed Soleyman on May 26, 1908, giving birth to the Anglo-Persian Oil Company (now BP).

BAZAAR-O WORLD.clue_en: This desert city in Kerman province is known as the pistachio capital of the world, home to colossal pistachio empires and the birthplace of statesman Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.
BAZAAR-O WORLD.expl_en: Rafsanjan's climate and water management via ancient subterranean qanats allowed it to become Iran's largest center of pistachio orchards and non-oil agricultural export revenue.

APADANA & APARTMENTS.clue_en: Begun around 518 BC by Darius the Great on a massive stone terrace, this ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire is known in Persian as Takht-e Jamshid.
APADANA & APARTMENTS.expl_en: Persepolis featured the monumental Gate of All Nations, the 100-Column Hall, and the Apadana Palace, where delegations from 23 nations brought tribute for Nowruz.

APADANA & APARTMENTS.clue_en: Consisting of a simple gabled limestone chamber atop a six-tiered stone plinth, this austere monument in Fars marks the final resting place of Cyrus the Great.
APADANA & APARTMENTS.expl_en: Alexander the Great reportedly visited the tomb in 330 BC, ordering it repaired after reading the epitaph: 'O man, I am Cyrus, who founded the Persian Empire; begrudge me not therefore this little earth that covers my body.'

APADANA & APARTMENTS.clue_en: Inaugurated in 1971 as the Shahyad Tower to mark the monarchy's 2,500th anniversary, this Tehran landmark combining Sasanian and Islamic arches was designed by 24-year-old architect Hossein Amanat.
APADANA & APARTMENTS.expl_en: Constructed from 25,000 blocks of white Isfahan marble, the monument was renamed Borj-e Azadi (Freedom Tower) after the massive demonstrations of the 1979 Revolution filled the square.

APADANA & APARTMENTS.clue_en: Completed in 1590 under Shah Abbas, this quintessential Persian paradise garden in Kashan features natural turquoise spring fountains and the bathhouse where Amir Kabir was assassinated.
APADANA & APARTMENTS.expl_en: Bagh-e Fin harnesses natural water pressure from the Soleymaniyeh Spring without mechanical pumps; in its hammam, royal assassins severed Amir Kabir's veins on January 10, 1852.

APADANA & APARTMENTS.clue_en: Built between 1302 and 1312 by Mongol Ilkhan Öljaitü in Zanjan province, this 49-meter turquoise-domed octagonal mausoleum is one of the world's oldest double-shelled brick domes, pre-dating Florence Cathedral.
APADANA & APARTMENTS.expl_en: The Dome of Soltaniyeh is an engineering marvel weighing 200 tons, whose double-shell design inspired Filippo Brunelleschi in his design of the Duomo of Florence.

GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.clue_en: Lecturing to thousands of students at Tehran's Husseiniyeh Ershad, this Sorbonne-educated sociologist energized revolutionary youth by contrasting dynamic 'Red Shi'ism' with passive 'Black Shi'ism'.
GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.expl_en: Dr. Ali Shariati (1933–1977) fused Marxist liberation theology with Shi'i martyrdom symbolism, turning Imam Hussein into a revolutionary archetype for the anti-monarchical struggle.

GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.clue_en: In a searing 1962 polemic that likened Western cultural and economic consumerism to a cholera outbreak or pestilence, Jalal Al-e Ahmad coined this Persian term.
GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.expl_en: In Gharbzadegi (Plagued by the West), Al-e Ahmad argued that Iran was like a wheat stalk infested by weevils, mindlessly consuming Western gadgets while abandoning its cultural soul.

GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.clue_en: Beyond his revolutionary satire, this constitutionalist spent forty-five years compiling the monumental Loghatnameh, the most comprehensive dictionary of the Persian language.
GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.expl_en: Dehkhoda's Loghatnameh spans over 26,000 pages across 50 volumes, documenting millions of citations, vocabulary, and historical biographies.

GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.clue_en: This outspoken secular historian of the Constitutional Revolution was assassinated inside a Tehran courtroom in 1946 by the fundamentalist group Fadayan-e Islam.
GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.expl_en: Ahmad Kasravi was on trial for 'slander of Islam' when brothers from Navvab Safavi's Fadayan-e Islam stabbed and shot him and his secretary inside the Palace of Justice.

GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.clue_en: In 1858, Mirza Malkom Khan organized this Masonic-style secret society in Tehran, whose literal Persian name means 'House of Oblivion' or 'House of Forgetfulness'.
GHARBZADEGI & GRIEVANCE.expl_en: Alarmed by reports of subversive republican teachings, Nasir al-Din Shah banned the Faramoushkhaneh in 1861 and exiled Malkom Khan to Baghdad.

COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.clue_en: Adapted from Gholam-Hossein Sa'edi's short story and starring Ezzatollah Entezami as a grieving villager who becomes his own cow, this 1969 Dariush Mehrjui film launched the Iranian New Wave.
COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.expl_en: Smuggled out of Iran to the 1971 Venice Film Festival where it won the FIPRESCI Critics' Prize, Gaav was praised even by Ayatollah Khomeini as an example of serious, healthy cinema.

COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.clue_en: Founded in 1965 under Queen Farah's patronage, this Center for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults became the incubator where Abbas Kiarostami directed his first films.
COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.expl_en: Kanun's filmmaking department, founded in 1969, gave directors like Kiarostami, Amir Naderi, and Bahram Beyzai artistic freedom and 35mm equipment without commercial interference.

COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.clue_en: In 1997, Abbas Kiarostami made history as the first Iranian filmmaker to win the Cannes Palme d'Or for this minimalist drama following a man driving around Tehran's dusty hills seeking someone to bury him.
COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.expl_en: Taste of Cherry tied with Shohei Imamura's The Eel at Cannes; when French actress Catherine Deneuve kissed Kiarostami on the cheek during the awards ceremony, it ignited controversy back in Tehran.

COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.clue_en: Because Iranian facilities lacked sound recording technology in 1933, Abdolhossein Sepanta travelled to this Indian port city to shoot Dokhtar-e Lor at Ardeshir Irani's Imperial Film Company.
COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.expl_en: Bombay was chosen because Ardeshir Irani had produced Alam Ara (India's first sound feature) there in 1931 and welcomed Sepanta to create the first Persian-language sound movie.

COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.clue_en: Named after the Quranic dawn surah and held annually every February to mark the anniversary of the revolution, this is Iran's highest cinematic award ceremony, presenting the Crystal Simurgh.
COWS, CHERRIES & CELLULOID.expl_en: Inaugurated in 1982, the Fajr Film Festival's prestigious prize is the Crystal Simurgh (Simorgh-e Bolurin), honoring excellence in directing, performance, and cinematography.

THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.clue_en: Signed in Saint Petersburg without consulting the Iranian government, this 1907 treaty between Britain and Russia carved Iran into northern Russian and southeastern British spheres of influence.
THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.expl_en: The 1907 convention ended the 'Great Game' between the British and Tsarist empires, leaving only a narrow neutral buffer strip across central Iran.

THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.clue_en: Concluding the Anglo-Persian War in March 1857, Nasir al-Din Shah was forced to sign this treaty in the French capital, formally relinquishing all Iranian claims to the city and kingdom of Herat.
THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.expl_en: British forces invaded Bushehr and Kharg Island in 1856 to force Iran out of Herat, ensuring Afghanistan remained a British buffer against Tsarist expansion toward India.

THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.clue_en: Lord Curzon drafted this secret August 1919 agreement that would have placed Iran's army and finances under British control, secured by massive secret bribes paid to Prime Minister Vosough al-Dowleh.
THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.expl_en: Outrage over the 130,000-toman bribe paid to Vosough al-Dowleh caused the Majles to reject the 1919 agreement and directly paved the way for Reza Khan's 1921 coup.

THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.clue_en: In October 1964, the Majles passed a bill granting diplomatic immunity and extraterritorial jurisdiction to this country's military personnel and their families in Iran, triggering Ayatollah Khomeini's deportation.
THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.expl_en: Khomeini delivered his furious October 26, 1964 speech condemning the bill, crying that the Shah had reduced Iranians to lower status than an American dog; he was arrested and flown to Turkey one week later.

THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.clue_en: Hired in 1911 by the Majles as Treasurer-General, this defiant American lawyer organized the Treasury Gendarmerie before Tsarist Russia issued an ultimatum sending troops to invade Tehran and expel him.
THE GREAT GAME OF THRONES.expl_en: Upon his forced expulsion, Shuster published the international bestseller 'The Strangling of Persia' (1912), exposing the brutal Anglo-Russian strangulation of Iranian constitutional democracy.

LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.clue_en: Rising to 5,609 meters in the Alborz mountain range, this snow-capped potentially active stratovolcano is the highest peak in Iran and the highest volcano in Asia.
LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.expl_en: Mount Damavand holds a mythic place in Persian literature, celebrated in modern poetry by Mohammad-Taqi Bahar: 'Ey Div-e Sepid-e Pay-dar-band' (O White Demon in Shackles).

LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.clue_en: Originating in the Zard-Kuh mountains and flowing through Ahvaz into the Arvand Rud, this 950-kilometer waterway is Iran's longest and only navigable river.
LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.expl_en: In 1888, Nasir al-Din Shah opened the Karun River to international navigation, allowing the British Lynch Brothers to operate commercial steamship routes into the Iranian interior.

LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.clue_en: Famed for its wind-sculpted yardangs (Kaluts) and recorded by NASA satellites as having the hottest land surface temperature on Earth (70.7°C), this salt desert lies in southeastern Iran.
LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.expl_en: Dasht-e Lut was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016; its abiotic Gandom Beryan plateau is one of the most hyper-arid zones on the planet.

LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.clue_en: Measuring only 39 kilometers wide at its narrowest passage between Iran and Oman, this strategic waterway accommodates twenty percent of global petroleum consumption.
LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.expl_en: Shah Abbas expelled the Portuguese from Hormuz in 1622 with English East India Company naval assistance, renaming the mainland port Gombroon as Bandar Abbas.

LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.clue_en: Once the second largest hypersaline lake in the world, this vanishing body of water between East and West Azerbaijan provinces is home to endemic Artemia brine shrimp.
LUT'S GET PHYSICAL.expl_en: Dam construction, excessive irrigation, and climate change caused Lake Urmia to shrink to less than ten percent of its former surface area, creating hazardous salt dust storms.

LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.clue_en: At the 1848 Badasht conference, this brilliant poet and Babi leader removed her veil before an assembly of shocked men, declaring before her execution: 'You can kill me as soon as you like, but you cannot stop the emancipation of women.'
LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.expl_en: Fatemeh Baraghani of Qazvin, conferred the title Tahirih ('The Pure One'), was executed by strangulation in the Ilkhani garden in Tehran in 1852.

LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.clue_en: In 1894, this satirical writer composed Ma'ayeb al-Rejal (The Vices of Men) in furious response to a patriarchal advice book, and in 1907 founded the Dushizegan School, Iran's first girls' school.
LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.expl_en: Bibi Khanoom established Dabestan-e Dushizegan in Tehran in 1907; when religious conservatives attacked it as a brothel, she rallied constitutionalists to protect it.

LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.clue_en: Daughter of Nasir al-Din Shah, this forward-thinking princess cast aside court confinement to play European piano, write Crowning Anguish (Khaterat), and champion constitutional democracy.
LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.expl_en: Taj al-Saltaneh's memoirs provide an uncensored look inside the royal harem, deploring dynastic corruption, foreign exploitation, and the subjection of Iranian women.

LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.clue_en: Set in WWII-occupied Shiraz and charting Zari's awakening to resistance following the murder of her husband Yusef, this 1969 novel by Simin Daneshvar was the first published by an Iranian woman.
opts_en: Tuba and the Meaning of Night
LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.expl_en: Savushun (evoking the ancient mourning rituals for Siavash) became the bestselling novel in modern Iranian history, translated into sixteen languages.

LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.clue_en: Dying of typhoid in 1941 at age 34, this poetess excelled in the didactic dialogue form (Monazereh), using allegorical debates between garlic and onion, or a king and an orphan.
LADIES OF THE CONSTITUTION.expl_en: Parvin E'tesami's Divan displays mastery of traditional Persian poetic forms to advance trenchant social criticism of poverty, greed, and the hollow vanity of rulers.

CYRUS ON ROLLS.clue_en: Discovered in Babylon in 1879 by Hormuzd Rassam and acclaimed by the United Nations as a pioneering charter of human rights, this 6th-century BC baked-clay artifact proclaimed the restoration of conquered shrines.
CYRUS ON ROLLS.expl_en: Issued after Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC, it permitted displaced peoples—including the Jewish exiles—to return to their homelands.

JOHANNESBURG BLUES.clue_en: Following the August 1941 Allied invasion of Iran, Reza Shah was forced to abdicate by the British and died in July 1944 in exile in this South African metropolis.
JOHANNESBURG BLUES.expl_en: Reza Shah died in a residence on Tenth Avenue in Parktown, Johannesburg; his embalmed body was initially sent to Cairo and later entombed in Rey.

JOHANNESBURG BLUES.clue_en: Following the August 1941 Allied invasion of Iran, Reza Shah was forced to abdicate by the British and died in July 1944 in exile in this South African metropolis.
JOHANNESBURG BLUES.expl_en: Reza Shah died in a residence on Tenth Avenue in Parktown, Johannesburg; his embalmed body was initially sent to Cairo and later entombed in Rey.

AIR FRANCE TO TEHRAN.clue_en: On February 1, 1979, ending fifteen years in exile, Ayatollah Khomeini flew from Paris to Tehran's Mehrabad Airport aboard a chartered Boeing 747 operated by this national carrier.
AIR FRANCE TO TEHRAN.expl_en: During the flight, American journalist Peter Jennings asked Khomeini what he felt returning to Iran after fifteen years; Khomeini's famous single-word reply was: 'Hichi' (Nothing).

AIR FRANCE TO TEHRAN.expl_en: During the flight, American journalist Peter Jennings asked Khomeini what he felt returning to Iran after fifteen years; Khomeini's famous single-word reply was: 'Hichi' (Nothing).

THE SHAH'S SIX POINTS.clue_en: In January 1963, Mohammad Reza Shah launched this sweeping 19-point program of social and economic modernization, whose primary pillar was land reform breaking up feudal estates.
THE SHAH'S SIX POINTS.expl_en: Spearheaded by Minister of Agriculture Hasan Arsanjani, the White Revolution redistributed feudal lands to millions of peasants and established the Literacy Corps (Sepah-e Danesh).
