AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.clue_en: In December 1945, backed by Soviet occupying troops, veteran communist Ja'far Pishevari proclaimed this autonomous regional government in Tabriz.
AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.expl_en: The Azerbaijan crisis of 1945–1946 was the first major international confrontation of the Cold War and the first dispute brought before the UN Security Council.

AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.clue_en: In early 1946, this wily veteran prime minister travelled to Moscow to outmaneuver Stalin, offering prospective northern oil concessions in exchange for complete Red Army withdrawal.
AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.expl_en: Qavam signed the Qavam-Sadchikov agreement in April 1946; once Soviet troops withdrew, the new Majles overwhelmingly rejected the oil concession, leaving Stalin empty-handed.

AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.clue_en: Founded in October 1941 by prominent leftist intellectuals known as the 'Fifty-Three', this pro-Soviet communist party became the best-organized political force in modern Iran.
AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.expl_en: The Tudeh Party ('Party of the Masses') built formidable labor unions among Khuzestan oil workers and railway men, as well as an extensive clandestine military officer network.

AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.clue_en: Proclaimed in January 1946 in Chahar Cheragh Square by Qazi Muhammad, this short-lived Soviet-sponsored Kurdish republic was defended by peshmerga under Mulla Mustafa Barzani.
AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.expl_en: The Republic of Mahabad lasted barely eleven months; after the Iranian army re-entered the region in December 1946, Qazi Muhammad was publicly hanged in Chahar Cheragh Square.

AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.clue_en: Signed in 1955 as the Baghdad Pact and renamed CENTO after the Iraqi revolution, this Western-backed military alliance anchored Iran with Turkey, Pakistan, and Britain as a 'Northern Tier' shield.
AZERBAIJAN CRISIS: 1946.expl_en: CENTO headquarters moved to Ankara in 1958 after the regicide of King Faisal II in Baghdad; Iran remained a member until withdrawal following the 1979 Revolution.

AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.clue_en: Known in the West as Avicenna, this 11th-century polymath from Bukhara authored The Canon of Medicine, which remained the standard medical textbook in Europe for five centuries.
AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.expl_en: Ibn Sina (980–1037 AD) synthesized Galenic and Aristotelian medicine in the five-volume Canon of Medicine (Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb).

AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.clue_en: Born in Rayy near modern Tehran, this 9th-century chemist and clinician was the first to clinically distinguish measles from smallpox and discover medical alcohol.
AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.expl_en: Abu Bakr Mohammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi authored the encyclopedic Kitab al-Hawi (The Comprehensive Book on Medicine).

AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.clue_en: Originating from Khwarazm, this 9th-century mathematician's treatise on balancing equations gave the world the word 'algebra' and introduced Arabic-Hindu numerals to Europe.
AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.expl_en: His book Al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala gave birth to the terms 'algebra' and 'algorithm'.

AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.clue_en: Accompanying Mahmud of Ghazni on his conquests in the 11th century, this universal genius calculated the radius and circumference of the Earth with 99% accuracy.
AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.expl_en: Abu Rayhan al-Biruni measured the dip of the horizon from a fort in Nandana (modern Pakistan) to compute the Earth's radius within 16 kilometers of modern values.

AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.clue_en: In 1079, this astronomer and poet led the committee that created the Jalali solar calendar, which remains more astronomically accurate than the Gregorian calendar.
AVICENNA & THE BRAINIACS.expl_en: Commissioned by Seljuk Sultan Jalal al-Din Malik-Shah, Khayyam calculated the year's length as 365.24219858156 days, an error of just one day every 5,000 years.

RUMI WITH A VIEW.clue_en: Fleeing the Mongol invasion from Balkh to Konya, this 13th-century mystic composed the 25,000-verse Masnavi after meeting the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz.
RUMI WITH A VIEW.expl_en: Mowlana Jalal al-Din Mohammad Rumi's Masnavi-ye Ma'navi is revered across the Persianate world as 'the Quran in Persian verse'.

RUMI WITH A VIEW.clue_en: An apothecary by trade who perished during the 1221 Mongol sack of Nishapur, this mystic allegorist wrote The Conference of the Birds (Mantiq al-Tayr).
RUMI WITH A VIEW.expl_en: In Mantiq al-Tayr, thirty birds (Si-morgh) journey through seven valleys in search of their divine king, realizing that they themselves are the Simurgh.

RUMI WITH A VIEW.clue_en: Executed in Baghdad in 922 AD for uttering the ecstatic utterance 'Ana al-Haqq' (I am the Truth), this mystic became the supreme martyr of Persian Sufism.
RUMI WITH A VIEW.expl_en: Hallaj's declaration was interpreted by orthodox jurists as a claim to divinity, but Sufis saw it as the ultimate extinction of ego (fana) in God.

RUMI WITH A VIEW.clue_en: This enigmatic, wild wandering mystic from Azerbaijan arrived in Konya in 1244, transforming a sober Islamic scholar into the ecstatic poet Rumi.
RUMI WITH A VIEW.expl_en: Shams vanished mysteriously in 1248, likely murdered by jealous disciples; in his grief, Rumi composed the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi in his friend's name.

RUMI WITH A VIEW.clue_en: Born in Khorasan in 804 AD, this master introduced the concept of Fana (annihilation of the self in God) and was famous for his ecstatic 'shathiyat' utterances.
RUMI WITH A VIEW.expl_en: Bayazid's tomb in Bastam (Semnan province) became a major pilgrimage center, inspiring generations of poets with his vision of divine ecstasy.

HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.clue_en: Completed in 1258 AD, this rhymed prose masterpiece of moral tales and maxims by Sa'di takes its name from the Persian word for 'rose garden'.
HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.expl_en: Sa'di's Golestan contains the famous poem inscribed at the entrance of the United Nations: 'Human beings are members of a whole, in related creation of one essence and soul.'

HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.clue_en: Built in the late 19th century in Shiraz, this Qajar garden features a majestic central pavilion, sour orange orchards, and a towering 200-year-old weeping cypress called Sarv-e Naz.
HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.expl_en: Bagh-e Eram (Garden of Paradise) was laid out by the Ilkhani paramount chiefs of the Qashqai confederacy before being acquired by the Qavam family of Shiraz.

HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.clue_en: Featuring magnificent stained glass that casts kaleidoscope patterns across Persian carpets each morning, this Shiraz landmark is known as the Pink Mosque.
HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.expl_en: Built between 1876 and 1888 by order of Qajar aristocrat Mirza Hasan Ali Nasir al-Mulk, its extensive pink ceramic rose tiles give it the moniker 'The Pink Mosque'.

HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.clue_en: Containing the tomb of Mir Sayyed Ahmad, brother of the Eighth Imam Reza, this holy shrine in Shiraz is famous for interior walls covered in millions of cut mirrors.
HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.expl_en: Shah Cheragh ('King of the Light') was given its moniker when queen Tashi Khatun built its great dome in the 14th century after a glowing light reportedly marked the martyr's grave.

HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.clue_en: Constructed in the 1760s with 48 solid carved spiral limestone columns and a marble pulpit carved from a single slab, this mosque forms the heart of Karim Khan Zand's complex.
HAFIZ THE BEATLES OF SHIRAZ.expl_en: The Vakil Mosque's 14-step minbar was hewn from solid green marble transported all the way from Maragheh in Azerbaijan by order of the Regent.

FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.clue_en: In 1786, after crushing rival khans, this eunuch founder of the Qajar dynasty proclaimed Tehran the official capital of Iran due to its proximity to his tribal base in Mazandaran.
FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.expl_en: Agha Mohammad Khan was crowned Shah in Tehran in 1796; at the time, Tehran was a fortified town of barely twenty thousand inhabitants surrounded by mud walls and watchtowers.

FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.clue_en: Featuring the Marble Throne (Takht-e Marmar) and the brilliant Hall of Mirrors (Talar-e Ayeneh), this historic royal walled complex in central Tehran is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.expl_en: Golestan Palace was the seat of Qajar power; in 1925, Reza Shah's coronation took place in its halls, as did the coronation of Mohammad Reza Shah in 1967.

FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.clue_en: Stretching over 18 kilometers from the central railway station north to Tajrish Square, this tree-lined thoroughfare is the longest street in the Middle East.
FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.expl_en: Constructed by order of Reza Shah in the 1930s to link the central marble palaces to his summer palace at Sa'dabad, it was originally named Pahlavi Avenue.

FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.clue_en: Completed in 2007 standing 435 meters tall, this telecommunications tower overlooking northwest Tehran is the sixth-tallest tower in the world.
FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.expl_en: Designed by architect Mohammad Reza Hafezi, Borj-e Milad features an octagonal pod with a revolving restaurant and observation deck offering panoramic views of the Alborz.

FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.clue_en: Located south of modern Tehran, this ancient city was mentioned in the Avesta as Rhaga and was the birthplace of Harun al-Rashid before being pulverized by the Mongols in 1220.
FROM VILLAGE TO VALIASR.expl_en: After the Mongol obliteration of Rayy, survivors relocated to the small northern neighboring agricultural village of Tehran, initiating its long rise to prominence.

QOM WHAT MAY.clue_en: Located in Mashhad, this sprawling 600,000-square-meter complex is the largest mosque in the world by area, surrounding the tomb of the Eighth Shi'i Imam.
QOM WHAT MAY.expl_en: Administered by the Astan-e Qods Razavi foundation, the shrine complex attracts over 25 million pilgrims annually from across the Islamic world.

QOM WHAT MAY.clue_en: The theological heart of Shi'i clerical training (Hawza) in Iran, this city's gold-domed shrine honors Hazrat Fatima Masumeh, sister of Imam Reza.
QOM WHAT MAY.expl_en: Fatima Masumeh died in Qom in 816 AD while traveling to visit her brother; her shrine was embellished with golden domes by Safavid and Qajar sovereigns.

QOM WHAT MAY.clue_en: This shrine in Rey south of Tehran served as the primary sanctuary (bast) where tobacco protesters in 1891, constitutionalists in 1905, and Nasir al-Din Shah's assassin took refuge.
QOM WHAT MAY.expl_en: Nasir al-Din Shah was shot inside the shrine of Shah Abdol-Azim on May 1, 1896, while praying on the eve of his golden jubilee.

QOM WHAT MAY.clue_en: Located near Qom, this mosque has become a massive pilgrimage center due to popular beliefs that the Twelfth Imam (the Mahdi) occasionally appears there.
QOM WHAT MAY.expl_en: Pilgrims drop written petitions into a sacred well (chah-e arizah) behind the mosque, a practice that expanded dramatically during the 2000s.

QOM WHAT MAY.clue_en: Built in 1418 by the Timurid empress of the same name inside the Imam Reza complex in Mashhad, this architectural jewel was the site of the 1935 massacre of anti-hat protesters.
QOM WHAT MAY.expl_en: Empress Goharshad, wife of Shahrukh, commissioned master architect Ghavameddin Shirazi; in July 1935, Reza Shah's troops fired machine guns inside, killing hundreds protesting Westernized dress.

TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.clue_en: Often proclaimed Iran's national dish, this slow-simmered herb stew combines parsley, cilantro, fenugreek, red kidney beans, and intensely sour sun-dried Persian limes (limoo amani).
TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.expl_en: Ghormeh Sabzi is celebrated for its deep emerald color and savory-sour taste derived from slow-caramelized herbs and dried limes from southern Iran.

TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.clue_en: Originating in Gilan and served at imperial banquets, this rich sweet-and-sour walnut stew is darkened with concentrated sour pomegranate molasses and slow-braised duck or chicken.
TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.expl_en: In Caspian cooking, Fesenjan is traditionally made with wild teal duck (morghe-abi), cooked for hours until walnut oils rise to the surface.

TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.clue_en: Cooked in traditional clay or stone pots (Dizi), this comforting lamb and chickpea broth is separated at the table: the broth is eaten with torn sangak bread, and the solids are pounded into a savory paste.
TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.expl_en: Eating Abgoosht is an interactive communal ritual involving a special heavy masher called a Goosht-koob to crush the meat, beans, and potatoes.

TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.clue_en: From the smoky kitchens of Gilan, this charred eggplant and tomato appetizer is vigorously mashed with abundant garlic and scrambled eggs, named after a Qajar governor of Rasht.
TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.expl_en: Mirza Qasim Khan Qajar, governor of Rasht under Nasir al-Din Shah, developed the recipe after experimenting in his private kitchen.

TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.clue_en: The crowning glory of Persian rice cookery, this golden, crunchy crust formed at the bottom of the pot is fiercely fought over at every family gathering.
TAHDIG YOUR OWN GRAVE.expl_en: Tahdig ('bottom of the pot') can be made with saffron-infused rice crust, sliced thin potatoes, flat lavash bread, or yogurt layers.

CARPET DIEM.clue_en: Centered in Isfahan, this exquisite metal art involves fusing vitreous colored enamel onto etched copper dishes and firing them at 800°C to create dazzling azure patterns.
CARPET DIEM.expl_en: The name derives from Mina (heaven/azure); Isfahani masters like Shokrollah Sanizadeh revived the craft in the 20th century.

CARPET DIEM.clue_en: Perfected in Shiraz, this delicate marquetry art involves assembling hundreds of thousands of microscopic polygonal rods of camel bone, brass, and rosewood into geometric stars.
CARPET DIEM.expl_en: A single square centimeter of high-grade Khatam can contain up to 250 micro-elements glued into intricate repeating geometric patterns.

CARPET DIEM.clue_en: Woven on traditional wooden looms in the desert city of Yazd, this luxurious hand-woven silk and wool brocade cloth often features the iconic Boteh Jegheh (paisley) motif.
CARPET DIEM.expl_en: Termeh weaving requires immense patience; historical weavers produced barely a few centimeters per day for royal court gowns and ceremonial dowries.

CARPET DIEM.clue_en: In Isfahan's grand bazaar, the rhythmic clinking of hammers against chisels marks this traditional art of hand-engraving and repoussé on silver, brass, and copper vessels.
CARPET DIEM.expl_en: Before carving, artisans pour hot melted pitch (Ghir) inside the vessel to absorb hammer blows and prevent the metal from puncturing.

CARPET DIEM.clue_en: Born in Herat around 1450, this supreme master painter of Persian miniatures revolutionized manuscript illumination with naturalistic movement in the Timurid and Safavid royal ateliers.
CARPET DIEM.expl_en: Behzad served Sultan Husayn Bayqara in Herat and was appointed director of the royal library in Tabriz by Shah Ismail I in 1522.

SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.clue_en: Established in 1957 with CIA and Mossad technical guidance, this notorious state security and intelligence service watched over every aspect of public life under the late Shah.
SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.expl_en: SAVAK wielded extrajudicial powers of interrogation, surveillance, and press censorship until disbanded by Shapour Bakhtiar in January 1979.

SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.clue_en: Appointed the first director of SAVAK in 1957, this ambitious general fell out with the Shah, fled to Iraq, and was assassinated in 1970 by SAVAK hitmen during a desert hunting trip.
SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.expl_en: Bakhtiar was shot in the Diyala desert in Iraq by a SAVAK double agent who had infiltrated his Iraqi-funded dissident entourage.

SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.clue_en: Built in the northern foothills of Tehran in 1972, this high-security fortress was designed by German engineers to house political prisoners and armed leftist guerrillas.
SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.expl_en: Evin featured soundproof interrogation cells and solitary confinement wings, becoming the primary symbol of state repression before the revolution.

SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.clue_en: Heading SAVAK for thirteen years from 1965 to 1978, this hardline general was arrested by the Shah as a sacrificial concession to protesters, only to be executed after the revolution.
SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.expl_en: Nassiri was executed on the roof of the Refah School on February 15, 1979, alongside three other imperial generals following summary trials by Sadegh Khalkhali.

SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.clue_en: Located near Tupkhaneh Square in the former Shahrbani lockup, this Joint Committee headquarters was notorious for brutal interrogation of guerrillas.
SAVAK TO THE FUTURE.expl_en: Now preserved as the Ebrat Museum (Museum of Warning), its circular layout prevented prisoners from orienting themselves during interrogation.

1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.clue_en: On August 19, 1978, over 400 moviegoers perished when the doors were locked and arsonists set ablaze this cinema in the southern oil city of Abadan, sparking nationwide outrage.
1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.expl_en: The audience was watching Masoud Kimiai's film The Deer (Gavaznha); the public blamed SAVAK, driving millions into active opposition to the monarchy.

1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.clue_en: On September 8, 1978 (17 Shahrivar), imperial soldiers opened fire on thousands of unarmed protesters gathered in this eastern Tehran square, an event forever known as Black Friday.
1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.expl_en: Military Governor Gholam-Ali Oveisi declared martial law just hours before troops opened fire in Jaleh Square (now Shohada Square), ending any hope of a negotiated compromise.

1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.clue_en: On January 7, 1978, this state newspaper published a libelous editorial under the pseudonym Ahmad Rashidi Motlagh slandering Khomeini, igniting the cycle of 40-day mourning protests.
1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.expl_en: The editorial labeled Khomeini an Indian agent and British pawn, sparking student riots in Qom on January 9 that were fired upon by police.

1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.clue_en: In October 1978, a crippling strike by 37,000 workers in this strategic industry choked off state oil revenues and gasoline supplies, breaking the financial spine of the regime.
1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.expl_en: Oil production plummeted from 6 million barrels per day to barely enough for domestic winter heating, forcing the Shah to impose military rule over the refineries.

1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.clue_en: On January 16, 1979, with tears in his eyes at Mehrabad Airport, this monarch boarded his Boeing 707 'Shahin' to depart Iran for an exile from which he would never return.
1978: A REVOLUTION ODYSSEY.expl_en: Newspapers famously hit the streets with the iconic massive two-word headline: 'SHAH RAFT' (The Shah Is Gone), triggering ecstatic celebrations across the nation.

TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.clue_en: In 53 BC at the Battle of Carrhae, this brilliant 30-year-old Parthian general decimated seven Roman legions using mounted horse archers and severed the head of Marcus Licinius Crassus.
TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.expl_en: Surena utilized the 'Parthian Shot' tactic—feigning retreat while firing arrows backwards over galloping horses—killing 20,000 Romans including Crassus.

TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.clue_en: Known as the Great and reigning from 124 to 91 BC, this Parthian king established diplomatic ties with Han Dynasty Emperor Wu of China, officially inaugurating the Silk Road.
TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.expl_en: Mithridates II revived the Achaemenid title 'King of Kings' (Shahanshah) on his coinage, stabilizing borders from Syria to Central Asia.

TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.clue_en: This tactical maneuver, made famous by nomadic steppe and Parthian cavalry, involved feigning a panicked retreat before twisting in the saddle to loose arrows backwards.
TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.expl_en: The maneuver entered the English language as 'a parting shot'—a cutting final remark made upon departure.

TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.clue_en: Located in modern Turkmenistan near Ashgabat, this fortified royal city was the first capital and ancestral necropolis of the Arsacid Parthian kings.
TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.expl_en: Excavations at UNESCO-listed Old Nisa uncovered magnificent rhytons (ivory drinking horns) combining Hellenistic craftsmanship with Persian motifs.

TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.clue_en: In 36 BC, this Roman triumvir invaded Parthian territory with 100,000 men seeking to avenge Crassus, but lost a third of his army in a disastrous mountain retreat through Media Atropatene.
TAKING A PARTHIAN SHOT.expl_en: King Phraates IV intercepted Antony's 300-wagon siege train at Phraaspa, forcing Antony into a retreat that echoed Xenophon's Anabasis.

DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.clue_en: Serving as chief minister from 1848 to 1851, Amir Kabir founded this pioneering modern polytechnic academy in Tehran to instruct students in engineering, military science, and medicine.
DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.expl_en: Dar al-Fonun opened in December 1851 with Austrian instructors, just days before Amir Kabir was executed in Fin Garden.

DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.clue_en: To inform the public and counter foreign imperial propaganda, Amir Kabir established this first official state newspaper in 1851.
DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.expl_en: Vaqaye-ye Ettefaqiyeh covered domestic administrative news, international world events, and public hygiene instructions.

DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.clue_en: Fighting religious superstition, Amir Kabir launched nationwide compulsory inoculation campaigns against this devastating epidemic disease that routinely blinded and killed children.
DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.expl_en: Amir Kabir weeping over children who died after traditional dervishes told parents vaccination was work of the devil is one of the most famous anecdotes in Iranian history.

DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.clue_en: Amir Kabir slashed the lavish royal pensions and corrupt allowances of this influential group: the Shah's court aristocrats, princes, and imperial harem members.
DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.expl_en: His reduction of royal court pensions made mortal enemies of the Queen Mother (Mahd-e Olia) and Mirza Aqa Khan Nuri, who convinced the Shah to execute him.

DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.clue_en: Dismissed in November 1851, Amir Kabir was exiled to this central Iranian oasis city before being murdered in its Fin Garden bathhouse.
DAR AL-FUN-UN & GAMES.expl_en: On January 10, 1852, royal executioner Ali Khan Hajeb al-Dowleh entered the bathhouse and cut his veins while he was bathing.

THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.clue_en: In November 1943, Churchill, Roosevelt, and Stalin met at the Soviet Embassy in Tehran for this secret summit code-named Eureka, planning Operation Overlord.
THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.expl_en: The Big Three signed the Declaration of the Three Powers Regarding Iran, promising to respect Iranian territorial integrity and independence after the war.

THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.clue_en: Because it served as the vital overland corridor transporting millions of tons of American Lend-Lease supplies to the Soviet front, Iran was hailed by this triumphant nickname.
THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.expl_en: Over 4 million tons of tanks, planes, fuel, and food were moved along the Trans-Iranian Railway to the Red Army, securing Soviet victory on the Eastern Front.

THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.clue_en: Evacuated from Soviet gulags in 1942 under General Władysław Anders, over 120,000 refugees from this European country were sheltered in camps across Tehran and Isfahan.
THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.expl_en: Isfahan earned the moniker 'City of Polish Children', where orphanages and schools were established; thousands of Polish graves remain in Doulab cemetery.

THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.clue_en: In December 1942, severe food hoarding, currency hyperinflation, and Allied requisition of grain sparked violent riots in Tehran over the shortage of this basic staple.
THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.expl_en: Protesters ransacked parliament and looted Prime Minister Ahmad Qavam's house when adulterated sawdust and gravel were discovered in Tehran bakeries.

THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.clue_en: On August 25, 1941, British and Soviet forces launched a surprise joint invasion of neutral Iran under this British military operation codename.
THE BRIDGE OF VICTORY ROAD.expl_en: Operation Countenance overwhelmed Iranian resistance in three days, resulting in the forced abdication of Reza Shah and Allied occupation until 1946.

ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.clue_en: Often hailed as the father of modern Persian short story writing, this diplomat penned the satirical 1921 collection Once Upon a Time (Yeki Bud, Yeki Nabud).
ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.expl_en: Jamalzadeh's preface to Yeki Bud, Yeki Nabud was a revolutionary literary manifesto demanding writers abandon flowery court rhetoric for natural vernacular Persian.

ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.clue_en: Published in 1952 while its author was imprisoned as a member of the leftist 'Fifty-Three', this romantic mystery novel centers on the enigmatic painting of a woman titled 'Her Eyes'.
ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.expl_en: Bozorg Alavi's Cheshmhayash follows the detective search for the identity of the dangerous femme fatale painted by revolutionary artist Master Makan.

ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.clue_en: Chronicling the generational decay of an aristocratic Qajar dynastic family through stream-of-consciousness, this haunting 1968 novella was written by Houshang Golshiri.
ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.expl_en: Adapted into an acclaimed 1974 film by Bahman Farmanara, Shazdeh Ehtejab is a devastating portrait of inherited cruelty and tuberculosis.

ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.clue_en: Stretching over 2,800 pages in ten volumes, this epic rural masterpiece by Mahmoud Dowlatabadi depicts the tragic struggle of the nomadic Kalmiši family in Khorasan.
ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.expl_en: Kelidar is the second longest novel in world literature, taking Dowlatabadi fifteen years to complete between 1970 and 1984.

ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.clue_en: Based on a real 1920s incident in Bushehr, this gripping 1963 revenge novel by Sadeq Chubak follows Zar Mohammad as he methodically murders the four corrupt notables who defrauded him.
opts_en: The Baboon Whose Buffoon Was Dead
ONCE UPON A JAMALZADEH.expl_en: Tangsir was adapted into a celebrated 1973 film directed by Amir Naderi, starring Behrouz Vossoughi as the Robin Hood-like avenger Shir Mohammad.

HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.clue_en: Serving as sole Marja-e Taqlid until his death in 1961, this conservative grand ayatollah rebuilt the Qom Hawza, avoiding direct political confrontation with the Shah.
HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.expl_en: Boroujerdi's death in March 1961 created a leadership vacuum that allowed the Shah to launch the White Revolution and prompted Khomeini's emergence.

HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.clue_en: In Najaf, this supreme Persian Marja issued decisive fatwas supporting the 1906 Constitution and declaring that obedience to Mohammad Ali Shah was war against God.
HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.expl_en: Khorasani mobilized support from Najaf; he died mysteriously in December 1911 on the eve of marching at the head of a volunteer army to expel Russian troops from Iran.

HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.clue_en: Based in Tabriz, this liberal Grand Ayatollah backed the 1979 Revolution but founded the Muslim People's Republic Party to oppose Velayat-e Faqih before being placed under house arrest.
HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.expl_en: Shariatmadari was stripped of his clerical rank in 1982 following allegations of complicity in Sadegh Ghotbzadeh's coup plot, dying under house arrest in 1986.

HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.clue_en: Forming an essential alliance with Mosaddegh before acrimoniously breaking with him in 1953, this populist Ayatollah served as Speaker of the 17th Majles.
HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.expl_en: Kashani feared Mosaddegh's secularism and flirtation with the communist Tudeh Party, welcoming General Zahedi's royalist coup in August 1953.

HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.clue_en: Refounding the Qom Seminary in 1922, this Grand Ayatollah protected the seminary through the aggressive secularization of the early Reza Shah years.
HAWZA LIFE TREATING YOU?.expl_en: Haeri Yazdi adopted strict political neutrality towards Reza Shah, ensuring the survival and financial autonomy of the Qom Hawza as a sanctuary for scholars.

FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.clue_en: Launched in March 1982 around Shush and Dezful, this massive joint operation liberated 2,500 square kilometers and routed three Iraqi divisions, paving the way to Khorramshahr.
FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.expl_en: Meaning 'Undeniable Victory' from Surah al-Fath, Fath ol-Mobin demonstrated the devastating tactical synergy between regular Artesh armor and volunteer Basij light infantry.

FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.clue_en: In February 1984, Iranian forces launched this daring amphibious assault across the Hawizeh Marshes using small fiberglass boats, capturing the oil-rich Majnoon Islands.
FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.expl_en: During Operation Kheibar, Iraq first deployed mustard gas and tabun nerve agent on a massive tactical scale against Iranian troops bogged down in the reeds.

FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.clue_en: In February 1986, Iranian commandos crossed the raging 1,000-meter-wide Arvand River in darkness to capture this strategic oil port on the Persian Gulf in Operation Valfajr-8.
FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.expl_en: The capture of Faw cut Iraq off from its coastline on the Persian Gulf and placed Iranian artillery within range of Kuwaiti airfields and oil refineries.

FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.clue_en: Fought in January 1987 in the fortified water obstacles of Fish Lake outside Basra, this meatgrinder battle was the single largest and bloodiest land battle of the war.
FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.expl_en: Iran breached three lines of the impregnable Soviet-designed 'Iron Ring' defenses around Basra, but suffered over 20,000 casualties in ferocious artillery barrages.

FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.clue_en: On September 23, 1980, hours after the Iraqi surprise invasion, 140 Iranian Air Force F-4 and F-5 fighter-bombers struck airfields across Iraq in this largest air raid in Iranian history.
FISH LAKE & TANK TRAPS.expl_en: Kaman 99 (Bow 99, referencing Arash the Archer's mythical shot) crippled Iraqi air bases and prevented Saddam from gaining air superiority over Khuzestan.

FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.clue_en: Narrated in his distinctive gravelly, poetic voice, this 63-episode television documentary series by Morteza Avini captured front-line frontline soldiers as mystical pilgrims on a sacred path.
FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.expl_en: Martyred by a landmine in Fakkeh in 1993, Avini was conferred the official title 'Master of the Martyr Intellectuals' (Seyed-e Shahidan-e Ahl-e Qalam).

FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.clue_en: Directed by Ebrahim Hatamikia in 1993, this emotional drama follows a chemical weapons victim sent to Germany for cornea surgery who encounters his estranged expatriate sister.
FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.expl_en: Featuring Majid Entezami's haunting pan-flute score, the film movingly humanized the trauma of 100,000 Iranian victims of Iraqi chemical attacks.

FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.clue_en: Directed by Bahram Beyzai in 1986 and shelved for three years, this lyrical anti-war masterpiece follows a dark-skinned boy fleeing southern bombardments who finds refuge with a Gilaki farm woman.
FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.expl_en: Starring Susan Taslimi as Na'i-Jan, the film championed linguistic and ethnic unity between Gilakis and southern Khuzestanis despite mutual incomprehension.

FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.clue_en: Narrated by 17-year-old Seyyedeh Zahra Hosseini, this massive 2008 bestselling memoir recounts her 20 days washing corpses and defending Khorramshahr during the Iraqi siege.
FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.expl_en: Da (meaning 'Mother' in Kurdish and Luri) became the fastest-selling book in post-revolutionary history, running through over 150 print editions.

FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.clue_en: Directed by Amir Naderi in 1984, this iconic New Wave film follows an illiterate orphan named Amiro who survives by shining shoes and collecting ice in the scorched ruins of war-era Abadan.
FROM KARKHEH WITH LOVE.expl_en: The Runner was the first post-revolutionary Iranian film to attract major global acclaim, winning the Golden Montgolfiere at the Three Continents Festival in Nantes.

REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.clue_en: Appointed Minister of Agriculture in 1961, this fiery radical lawyer was the intellectual architect of the land reform program that broke the power of feudal landlords.
REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.expl_en: Arsanjani's radical populism alarmed the Shah, who feared the charismatic minister would eclipse the throne; he was forced out as ambassador to Rome in 1963.

REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.clue_en: Created under Point Two of the White Revolution, this uniformed corps sent high school graduate conscripts into remote villages to teach rural children how to read and write.
REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.expl_en: Sepah-e Danesh deployed over 100,000 young men and women into 40,000 villages, dramatically raising national rural literacy rates between 1963 and 1978.

REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.clue_en: In June 1963 (15 Khordad), bloody riots erupted across Tehran and Qom after the Shah arrested Ayatollah Khomeini for denouncing land reform and this controversial social measure.
REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.expl_en: Prime Minister Asadollah Alam ordered troops to shoot to kill, crushing the 15 Khordad uprising with hundreds of casualties and solidifying Khomeini's status as the chief dissident.

REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.clue_en: Serving as Prime Minister for a record twelve years and six months from 1965 to 1977, this pipe-smoking Francophile statesman was famous for his fresh orchid lapel flowers.
REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.expl_en: Hoveyda presided over Iran's petrodollar economic boom; he was executed on April 7, 1979, after a summary trial by revolutionary judge Sadegh Khalkhali.

REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.clue_en: On March 2, 1975, the Shah dissolved all existing parliamentary political parties, declaring that all citizens must join this newly created single totalitarian party or leave the country.
REVOLUTION OF THE SHAH & PEOPLE.expl_en: Rastakhiz ('Resurgence') alienated the traditional bazaar by opening branches to enforce arbitrary price controls, accelerating middle-class participation in the revolution.

SIAHKAL & HYDE.clue_en: On February 8, 1971, thirteen young Marxist guerrillas attacked a gendarmerie post in this forested village in Gilan, inaugurating modern armed urban guerrilla warfare in Iran.
SIAHKAL & HYDE.expl_en: The Siahkal incident led to the formation of the Organization of Iranian People's Fedai Guerrillas (Cherikha-ye Fadai-e Khalq), immortalized in poem and song.

SIAHKAL & HYDE.clue_en: The chief theoretician of the Fadayan-e Khalq who wrote Armed Struggle: Both a Strategy and a Tactic, this intellectual was assassinated alongside eight others in Evin in 1975.
SIAHKAL & HYDE.expl_en: SAVAK officers took Jazani and eight fellow prisoners to the hills behind Evin Prison in April 1975 and machine-gunned them, claiming they had been 'shot while escaping'.

SIAHKAL & HYDE.clue_en: During his televised 1974 military tribunal, this Marxist poet electrified the country by proudly defending Che Guevara, Karl Marx, and Imam Hussein before refusing to ask for royal clemency.
SIAHKAL & HYDE.expl_en: Golsorkhi told the military judges: 'I found the first lessons of socialism in Islam and in the life of Imam Hussein.' He was executed on February 18, 1974.

SIAHKAL & HYDE.clue_en: Authored by Azeri teacher Samad Behrangi in 1968, this allegorical children's fable about a tiny fish swimming from a stream to the ocean became a banned sacred text for armed rebels.
opts_en: The Old Man and the Sea
SIAHKAL & HYDE.expl_en: Illustrated by Farshid Mesghali (who won the prestigious Hans Christian Andersen Award), the book warned children that conformity meant death.

SIAHKAL & HYDE.clue_en: Founded in 1965 by student intellectuals Hanifnejad, Saadati, and Badizadegan, this armed movement fused Islam with Marxist class analysis before fracturing into rival factions.
SIAHKAL & HYDE.expl_en: In 1975, a violent Marxist faction assassinated rival leaders and purged the Islamic wing, until Massoud Rajavi rebuilt the organization from inside prison.

TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.clue_en: As Crown Prince and governor of Tabriz, this tragic reformer commanded Iranian forces throughout both wars with Russia, creating the Western-drilled Nezam-e Jadid army.
TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.expl_en: Abbas Mirza died of kidney disease in Mashhad in 1833 at age 44, never ascending the throne, mourned as Iran's greatest military patriot.

TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.clue_en: Signed in October 1813 following the catastrophic rout at the Battle of Aslanduz, this treaty forced Iran to cede Georgia, Dagestan, and northern Azerbaijan to the Russian Empire.
TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.expl_en: The Treaty of Golestan also granted Russia the exclusive right to maintain naval warships on the Caspian Sea, turning it into a Russian lake.

TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.clue_en: In January 1829, an enraged Tehran mob stormed the Russian Legation and massacred this famous playwright and Tsarist ambassador for sheltering two escaped Armenian women.
TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.expl_en: Griboyedov, author of Woe from Wit, had insisted on strictly enforcing the humiliating terms of Turkmenchay; to avert war, the Shah sent the 88-carat Shah Diamond to Tsar Nicholas I.

TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.clue_en: Nicknamed 'the Dragon' for his ruthlessness, this Georgian nobleman and Russian commander-in-chief conquered Ganja in 1804 before being assassinated outside the gates of Baku in 1806.
TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.expl_en: During parleys outside Baku, Huseyngulu Khan's cousin drew a pistol and shot Tsitsianov; his severed head was dispatched as a trophy to Fath-Ali Shah in Tehran.

TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.clue_en: On October 31, 1812, Russian forces under General Pyotr Kotlyarevsky staged a night bayonet surprise attack across the Aras River, annihilating Abbas Mirza's camp at this battle.
TURKMEN-CHAY TEA PARTY.expl_en: The defeat at Aslanduz destroyed Iran's modernized artillery corps and compelled Fath-Ali Shah to sign the humiliating Treaty of Golestan the following year.

PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.clue_en: In October 1971, the Shah staged the most lavish party in modern history at Persepolis to celebrate this milestone anniversary of the Persian monarchy.
PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.expl_en: The 2,500-Year Celebration of the Persian Empire welcomed 60 monarchs, presidents, and heads of state to the ruins of Persepolis.

PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.clue_en: Catering for the Persepolis gala was entrusted exclusively to this legendary Parisian luxury restaurant, flying 150 chefs and waitstaff to the desert.
PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.expl_en: Maxim's shut down its Paris restaurant for two weeks to serve peacocks on royal porcelain and 25,000 bottles of vintage 1959 Dom Pérignon.

PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.clue_en: Heads of state stayed in an air-conditioned 'Tent City' arranged in five radiating avenues, custom designed by this prestigious French interior design firm.
PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.expl_en: Maison Jansen built 50 prefabricated apartment tents draped in French silk and tapestries, each with marble bathrooms and direct international telex.

PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.clue_en: At the tomb of Cyrus the Great in Pasargadae, the Shah delivered his famous proclamation opening: 'O Cyrus, King of Kings, rest in peace, for...'
PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.expl_en: The phrase 'Kourosh bekhab ke ma bidarim' became the defining rhetorical symbol of Pahlavi monarchical continuity with pre-Islamic antiquity.

PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.clue_en: From his exile in Najaf, Ayatollah Khomeini furiously condemned the festival as the 'Celebration of the Devil' in this recorded sermon.
PARTY LIKE IT'S 539 BC.expl_en: Khomeini lambasted the $100 million expenditure, crying that Iranians were starving in Fars while European monarchs ate roast peacock.

ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.clue_en: Spanning a deep mountain gorge in the Alborz at an altitude of 2,140 meters, this 110-meter-high masonry arch bridge is the masterpiece of the northern railway line.
ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.expl_en: Constructed by Austrian and Italian master masons under Danish engineering supervisor Jørgen Saxild, Hitler reportedly demanded its demolition during WWII to sever Soviet supply lines.

ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.clue_en: This Danish engineering consortium was contracted in 1933 by Reza Shah to oversee construction of the Trans-Iranian Railway, completing it nine months ahead of schedule.
ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.expl_en: Kampsax divided the mountainous terrain into 43 lots sub-contracted to French, Italian, and Swiss firms, employing up to 55,000 workers at a time.

ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.clue_en: The northern terminus of the Trans-Iranian Railway was established at this newly created port on the Caspian Sea in Mazandaran, renamed Bandar-e Torkaman in 1979.
ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.expl_en: Bandar-e Shah was connected via rail directly to Bandar-e Shahpur (now Bandar-e Imam Khomeini) on the Persian Gulf.

ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.ans_en: The Three Golden Lines (Seh Khat-e Tala)
ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.clue_en: Because trains could not climb the steep mountain gradient directly, engineers designed this breathtaking spiral series of three stacked loops near Gadook pass.
opts_en: The Three Golden Lines (Seh Khat-e Tala)
ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.expl_en: A passenger looking out the train window could see the same railway line stacked at three different elevations on the mountainside.

ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.clue_en: To finance the monumental 1,394-kilometer railway without foreign loans, Minister of Finance Ali-Akbar Davar enacted state monopolies on these two imported household commodities.
ALL ABOARD THE VERESK EXPRESS.expl_en: Passed by the Fifth Majles in May 1925, the sugar and tea monopoly tax ensured complete financial independence from British and Russian banks.

SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.clue_en: Holding the Khiyaban district of Tabriz alongside Sattar Khan during the 1908–1909 Royalist siege, this hero was acclaimed with the title Salar-e Melli (National Leader).
SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.expl_en: Baqer Khan was a stonemason and mayor of the Khiyaban quarter whose courage prevented royalist troops under Rahim Khan from crushing the revolution.

SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.clue_en: A young American Presbyterian teacher at the Memorial School in Tabriz, this 24-year-old resigned his post to join the constitutionalists and was shot dead leading a sortie against the siege.
SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.expl_en: Baskerville declared: 'The only difference between me and these people is my place of birth, and that is not a big difference.' He was buried as a national martyr in Tabriz.

SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.clue_en: An electrical engineer born in Urmia and trained in Tbilisi, this radical terrorist introduced bomb-making to the revolution and organized the assassination of Premier Atabak-e Azam in 1907.
SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.expl_en: Heydar Khan joined the Bolsheviks in Baku and later helped establish the Soviet Republic of Gilan before dying mysteriously in 1921.

SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.clue_en: In December 1911, Tsarist Russian troops invaded Tabriz following the Shuster ultimatum, publicly hanging the city's senior cleric on Ashura.
SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.expl_en: Mirza Ali Aqa Seqat ol-Eslam was hanged on the sacred day of Ashura for refusing to sign a manifesto claiming the Russian invasion was welcomed by the population.

SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.clue_en: This brilliant Armenian revolutionary commander led volunteer cavalry from the Caucasus to Rasht and spearheaded the July 1909 march that liberated Tehran from Royalist forces.
SATTAR WARS: TABRIZ STRIKES BACK.expl_en: Yeprem Khan was appointed police chief of Tehran after the victory; he was killed in battle against royalist rebels near Hamadan in May 1912.

IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.clue_en: Author of The Garden of Mirrors and Fresh Air (Hava-ye Tazeh), this titan of modern Iranian literature created She'r-e Sepid (White Verse), abandoning all rhyme and classical meter.
IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.expl_en: Writing under the pen-name A. Bamdad, Shamlou translated Lorca and Eluard and compiled the monumental multi-volume folklore encyclopedia Ketab-e Koucheh.

IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.clue_en: A painter and poet from Kashan who wrote Water's Footfall (Seda-ye Pay-e Ab), his luminous, Zen-like verse opens: 'I am from Kashan, my trade is painting...'
IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.expl_en: Sepehri's Eight Books (Hasht Ketab) synthesized Far Eastern Taoism and Sufi illumination, famous for the line: 'Eyes must be washed; things must be seen differently.'

IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.clue_en: Writing under the pen-name M. Omid, this master of the Khorasani epic style captured the crushing post-1953 coup depression in his celebrated masterpiece Zemestan (The Winter).
IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.expl_en: Opening with 'They will not answer your greeting; heads are buried in cloaks', Zemestan became the immortal national elegy for the crushed democratic hopes of the Mosaddegh era.

IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.clue_en: Known as the 'Lioness of Iran', this twentieth-century poetess revolutionized the classical ghazal by introducing modern colloquial rhythms and political defiance against tyranny.
IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.expl_en: Nominated twice for the Nobel Prize in Literature, Behbahani penned the defiant anthem 'I Will Rebuild You, My Homeland' (Dobareh misazamet, vatan).

IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.clue_en: Renowned for his romantic masterpiece Koucheh (The Alley), this beloved 20th-century poet wrote lyrical verse celebrated for its emotional gentleness and accessibility.
IT'S NIMA OR NEVER.expl_en: Moshiri's poem begins: 'Without you, once again at night, I wandered through that alley...', memorized by generations of Iranians.

DESERT ONE & DONE.ans_en: Muslim Student Followers of the Imam's Line
DESERT ONE & DONE.clue_en: On November 4, 1979, hundreds of radical Islamist university students stormed the US Embassy in Tehran, seizing 52 American diplomats under this official group name.
opts_en: Muslim Student Followers of the Imam's Line
DESERT ONE & DONE.expl_en: The students claimed the embassy was a 'Den of Spies' (Jasouskhaneh) plotting a repeat of the 1953 CIA coup, holding the hostages for 444 days.

DESERT ONE & DONE.clue_en: Serving as the public English-language spokesperson for the student hostage-takers and nicknamed 'Mary' by Western media, this woman later became Iran's first female Vice President.
DESERT ONE & DONE.expl_en: Educated in the United States as a child, Ebtekar later headed the Department of the Environment under Presidents Khatami and Rouhani.

DESERT ONE & DONE.clue_en: On April 24, 1980, President Jimmy Carter's military rescue mission Operation Eagle Claw ended in disaster when a helicopter collided with an EC-130 aircraft in this remote desert.
DESERT ONE & DONE.expl_en: A sudden sandstorm (haboob) blinded US pilots; eight American servicemen died, and the disaster doomed Carter's reelection campaign.

DESERT ONE & DONE.clue_en: In protest of the embassy takeover, this veteran statesman and first Prime Minister of the Islamic Republic resigned alongside his entire cabinet on November 6, 1979.
DESERT ONE & DONE.expl_en: Bazargan lamented that his provisional government was 'a knife without a blade' while real power was wielded by Khomeini and the Revolutionary Council.

DESERT ONE & DONE.clue_en: Brokered by Algerian diplomats, the 52 American hostages were finally released on January 20, 1981, minutes after this US president concluded his inaugural address.
DESERT ONE & DONE.expl_en: The Algiers Accords unwove frozen Iranian assets and barred future US military intervention in internal Iranian affairs in exchange for the hostages' release.

BULLET AT THE BAST.clue_en: On May 1, 1896, on the eve of his golden jubilee, Nasir al-Din Shah was assassinated inside the shrine of Shah Abdol-Azim by this disciple of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani.
BULLET AT THE BAST.expl_en: Mirza Reza was hanged in Tupkhaneh Square in August 1896; his pistol shot ended the 48-year reign of Nasir al-Din Shah.

LIAKHOV'S CANNONS.clue_en: On June 23, 1908, Mohammad Ali Shah ordered the Persian Cossack Brigade under this Russian colonel to bombard the Baharestan parliament building with artillery.
LIAKHOV'S CANNONS.expl_en: The shelling of the First Majles initiated the 'Little Autocracy' (Estebdad-e Saghir) that ended when constitutionalist armies took Tehran in 1909.

EXACTLY MIDNIGHT.clue_en: At midnight on August 15, 1953, the BBC Persian service signaled to the Shah that London supported the coup by changing its standard sign-on phrase to this exact five-word announcement.
EXACTLY MIDNIGHT.expl_en: The standard phrase was 'It is now midnight'; adding the word 'exactly' (daqiqan) confirmed Churchill's final authorization to the Shah.

DEHKHODA'S DEAD CANDLE.ans_en: Yad Ar, Ze Sham-e Morde, Yad Ar
DEHKHODA'S DEAD CANDLE.clue_en: Following the execution of Sur-e Esrafil co-founder Mirza Jahangir Khan in 1908, Ali-Akbar Dehkhoda penned this immortal elegy opening: 'Remember, of the dead candle, remember!'
opts_en: Yad Ar, Ze Sham-e Morde, Yad Ar
DEHKHODA'S DEAD CANDLE.expl_en: Dehkhoda dreamed of Jahangir Khan dressed in white saying: 'Why didn't you say that I died young?', waking in tears to compose the poem in Swiss exile.

VAULT OF CTESIPHON.clue_en: Standing 37 meters high near Baghdad, this monumental single-span unreinforced parabolic brick arch was the throne room (Iwan) of Sasanian King Khosrow I.
VAULT OF CTESIPHON.expl_en: Celebrated in Arabic and Persian poetry by Khaqani ('Behold the mirror of warning in the Iwan of Mada'in'), it is the largest single-span unreinforced brick vault in the world.

THE JAMEH RESISTANCE.clue_en: Standing as the defiant symbol of resistance throughout the 34-day battle and 575-day Iraqi occupation, this turquoise-domed building was the first landmark visited upon liberation.
THE JAMEH RESISTANCE.expl_en: The mosque served as command headquarters, weapons depot, and hospital; soldiers famously sang Jahanara's mourning song on its steps on May 24, 1982.

THALWEG BLUES.expl_en: Saddam tore up the Algiers Accord on live Iraqi television in September 1980, citing the river boundary as the primary casus belli for invading Iran.

SEA OF LIGHT DIAMOND.expl_en: Its name translates to 'Sea of Light'; gemologists believe it was cut from the Great Table Diamond seen by Tavernier in Golconda in 1642.

GOLNAR ON CELLULOID.expl_en: Saminejad faced severe family ostracism and harassment in conservative Tehran after the premiere, living in seclusion under an assumed name until her death in 1997.

SHUSTER'S INDICTMENT.expl_en: Shuster's book opened with the memorable line: 'It was the European policy of Russia and Great Britain in Persia to destroy the independence of a nation.'

TUS MARBLE CONGRESS.expl_en: Karim Taherzadeh Behzad designed the mausoleum in Achaemenid stone style, embodying Reza Shah's nationalist renaissance of pre-Islamic architectural heritage.

FEREYDUN'S OX-MACE.clue_en: In the Shahnameh, this righteous prince united with Kaveh the Blacksmith to overthrow the serpent tyrant Zahhak, chaining him beneath Mount Damavand.
FEREYDUN'S OX-MACE.expl_en: Fereydun struck Zahhak with his ox-headed mace (Gorz-e Gavsar), establishing the ancient autumn festival of Mehregan.

THE 300 & THEN SOME.clue_en: In 490 BC, Athenian hoplites under Miltiades repulsed the amphibious landing force of Darius the Great on this coastal plain 26 miles northeast of Athens.
THE 300 & THEN SOME.expl_en: The defeat marked the first time an Achaemenid imperial invasion force was repulsed on the Greek mainland, giving rise to the modern marathon race.

THE 300 & THEN SOME.clue_en: In 480 BC, Xerxes I's army was delayed at this narrow coastal pass by Spartan King Leonidas and his 300 hoplites before an encircling goat path was revealed.
THE 300 & THEN SOME.expl_en: After a local Greek named Ephialtes showed the Persians the Anopaia mountain path, the Immortals outflanked the Greeks, allowing Xerxes to advance on Athens.

THE 300 & THEN SOME.clue_en: Watching from a golden throne atop Mount Aigaleo, Xerxes saw his vast Phoenician and Persian armada outmaneuvered and destroyed by Greek triremes in this strait.
THE 300 & THEN SOME.expl_en: Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into narrow waters where their numerical advantage was negated, compelling Xerxes to withdraw to Asia.

THE 300 & THEN SOME.clue_en: In 401 BC, Cyrus the Younger rebelled against his brother Artaxerxes II with 10,000 Greek mercenaries at this battle, immortalized in Xenophon's Anabasis.
THE 300 & THEN SOME.expl_en: Cyrus was killed in the battle; the stranded Greek mercenaries (The Ten Thousand) marched across thousands of miles of hostile Persian territory to reach the Black Sea.

THE 300 & THEN SOME.clue_en: In 330 BC, satrap Ariobarzanes and his sister Youtab held this narrow pass in the Zagros Mountains with 700 men, ambushing Alexander the Great's army with avalanches.
THE 300 & THEN SOME.expl_en: Hailed as the 'Persian Thermopylae', Ariobarzanes fought to the last man until a local shepherd guided Alexander around the pass to Persepolis.

ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.clue_en: In the final trial of Rostam's Seven Labors (Haft Khan), Rostam slays this demonic king of Mazandaran inside a dark cavern, using its blood to restore King Kay Kavus's eyesight.
ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.expl_en: Rostam cut out the White Demon's liver, dripping its warm bile into the blinded eyes of the captive Iranian knights to restore their sight.

ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.clue_en: This shape-shifting demon transformed into a wild golden zebra, hurled a slumbering Rostam into the Caspian Sea, and possessed the power to turn stone into water.
ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.expl_en: When Akvan asked Rostam whether he preferred to be cast into the mountains or the sea, Rostam used reverse psychology, knowing demons always do the opposite.

ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.clue_en: In his third labor, Rostam was awakened in the wilderness three times by his stallion Rakhsh before slaying this colossal venomous monster.
ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.expl_en: The eighty-meter dragon made itself invisible whenever Rostam opened his eyes, until Rakhsh trampled it and Rostam severed its head with his ox-head mace.

ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.clue_en: In pre-Islamic Iranian mythology and the Shahnameh, this divine, glowing halo of royal fortune and destiny legitimizes kings and departs when they succumb to hubris.
ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.expl_en: King Jamshid lost the divine Farr (Farr-e Izadi) when he boasted that he was greater than God, causing his kingdom to fall to the tyrant Zahhak.

ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.clue_en: This Turanian king is the lifelong arch-nemesis of Iran in the Shahnameh, repeatedly invading the realm and ordering the murder of Prince Siavash.
ROSTAM'S SEVEN HABITS.expl_en: Afrasiyab reigned over Turan for centuries through sorcery until captured in Lake Chichast by the hermit Hom and executed by King Kay Khosrow.

MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.clue_en: Born in Shiraz in 1571 and teaching at Khan Madrasa, this supreme philosopher synthesized Avicennian Peripateticism and Suhrawardi's Illuminationism into Transcendent Theosophy.
MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.expl_en: Sadr al-Din Mohammad Shirazi (Mulla Sadra) founded Hikmat al-Muta'aliyah, positing the primacy of existence (Asalat al-Wujud) over essence.

MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.clue_en: Considered Mulla Sadra's magnum opus, this massive philosophical treatise in nine volumes takes its title from 'The Four Intellectual Journeys of the Soul'.
MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.expl_en: The four journeys trace the soul's path: from creation to God, in God, from God back to creation with God, and among creation to guide humanity.

MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.clue_en: Known as the 'Third Teacher' after Aristotle and Al-Farabi, this eccentric master in Isfahan solved the creation of the universe with his theory of Huduth-e Dahri (At-Temporal Origination).
MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.expl_en: Mir Damad was revered by Shah Abbas I, who famously walked beside his horse through the streets of Isfahan to demonstrate royal reverence for philosophy.

MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.clue_en: Born in Baalbek (Lebanon) and brought to Iran as a child, this polymath and architect designed the hydraulic heating of the Sheikh Bahai bathhouse using a single candle.
MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.expl_en: Sheikh Baha al-Din al-Amili also engineered the division of the Zayandeh River's waters across the districts of Isfahan (Tomar-e Sheikh Bahai).

MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.clue_en: Compiling the 110-volume hadith encyclopedia Bihar al-Anwar (Oceans of Light), this influential late Safavid cleric suppressed philosophy and Sufism under Shah Sultan Husayn.
MULLA SADRA'S SOUL FOOD.expl_en: Majlisi's strict clerical legalism marginalized religious minorities and contributed to the social ossification that preceded the Afghan conquest in 1722.

GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.clue_en: Measuring 1,491 square kilometers in the Strait of Hormuz, this dolphin-shaped island is the largest island in the Persian Gulf, famous for Hara mangrove forests.
GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.expl_en: Qeshm features the UNESCO Global Geopark, the Stars Valley (Darreh-ye Setaregan), and the Chahkooh Gorge carved by erosion.

GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.clue_en: Transformed in the 1970s into a duty-free luxury haven with a Grand Casino and supersonic Concorde flights, this 91-square-kilometer coral island lies in the Persian Gulf.
GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.expl_en: Kish remains a major visa-free shopping and tourism free-trade zone, famous for the scenic wreck of the Greek Cargo Ship grounded on its coral reefs in 1966.

GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.clue_en: Handling over ninety percent of all Iranian crude oil exports via deepwater sea berths, this fortified rocky island was bombed over 2,800 times by Iraqi jets during the war.
GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.expl_en: Kharg Island was shielded by Hawk anti-aircraft missile batteries and heroic repair crews who kept oil pumping onto tankers throughout the eight-year Tanker War.

GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.clue_en: Renowned for its red ochre beaches and rainbow-colored salt canyons, this tiny island features the ruins of an imposing 16th-century fortress built by Afonso de Albuquerque.
GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.expl_en: Hormuz Island was the commercial pearl of the Indies until Safavid commander Imam Quli Khan expelled the Portuguese garrison in 1622.

GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.clue_en: Originally named Gombroon and developed into Iran's primary container shipping port by Shah Abbas I, this coastal metropolis looks out over the Strait of Hormuz.
GULF OF PERSIA, NOT DISCORD.expl_en: Home to the Shahid Rajaee container terminal, Bandar Abbas handles over half of Iran's maritime sea trade today.

DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..clue_en: A towering playwright and director of Death of Yazdgerd and Bashu, the Little Stranger, this auteur is the grandmaster of historical allegorical theatre and film.
DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..expl_en: Beyzai's research into pre-Islamic dramatic traditions culminated in his monumental book A Study of Iranian Theatre (1965).

DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..clue_en: Known as the 'poet of Iranian cinema' for his lyrical historical dialogues, this director created the immortal TV epic Hezar Dastan and the beloved tearjerker Mother (Madar).
DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..expl_en: Hatami built the famous Ghazali Cinema Town in west Tehran to recreate 1930s Lalezar Street and the Tupkhaneh square for his cinematic works.

DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..clue_en: Directing Still Life (1974) and A Simple Event, this pioneer of international cinematic minimalism emigrated to Germany and inspired directors like Chantal Akerman and Jim Jarmusch.
DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..expl_en: Still Life won the Silver Bear at the 1974 Berlin Film Festival, featuring an aging railway switchman told he is being retired after 33 years of routine.

DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..clue_en: Directing A Separation (2011) and The Salesman (2016), this contemporary master became the only Iranian director to win two Academy Awards for Best Foreign Language Film.
DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..expl_en: A Separation also made history as the first foreign-language screenplay nominated for Best Original Screenplay at the Oscars.

DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..clue_en: This director won the Golden Leopard at Locarno for The Mirror (1997) and the Golden Bear at Berlin for Taxi (2015), despite being sentenced to a 20-year ban on filmmaking.
DIRECTED BY KIAROSTAMI & CO..expl_en: Panahi smuggled his film This Is Not a Film (2011) to the Cannes Film Festival hidden inside a USB flash drive baked inside a birthday cake.

JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.clue_en: Persian classical music is organized into this comprehensive canon of melodic motifs (Goushehs), arranged across seven primary modal systems (Dastgahs).
JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.expl_en: Preserved by 19th-century court masters Mirza Abdollah and Aqa Hossein-Qoli, the Radif was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009.

JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.clue_en: Revered as the undisputed 'Master' (Ostad) of Persian vocal music, this legendary baritone spent six decades mesmerizing millions with his breathtaking Tahrir vocal ornamentation.
JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.expl_en: Shajarian's unaccompanied prayer 'Rabbana' was broadcast at sundown every Ramadan on Iranian radio for thirty years, becoming a sacred national soundscape.

JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.clue_en: Held vertically and played by directing air between the upper incisors and the tongue (Dandan technique), this end-blown reed flute was played with peerless virtuosity by Hasan Kasaei.
JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.expl_en: The Ney opens Rumi's Masnavi with the immortal lament: 'Beshno az ney chon hekayat mikonad' (Listen to the reed as it tells its tale of separation).

JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.clue_en: Featuring a waist carved from solid mulberry wood covered in lamb fetus skin, this premier 25-fret long-necked lute is played with a brass plectrum encased in bee's wax.
JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.expl_en: Renowned luthiers like Yahya of Isfahan in the early 20th century carved instruments whose resonance remains the gold standard in Iranian music.

JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.clue_en: Featuring 72 strings arranged in courses of four over 18 movable bridges, this trapezoidal wooden hammered dulcimer was brought to modern perfection by Ostad Faramarz Payvar.
JUST FOR THE DASTGAH OF IT.expl_en: The Santur is played using two delicate featherweight wooden hammers (mezrab), producing a crystalline, shimmering soundscape.

STARS OVER MARAGHEH.clue_en: Grandson of Genghis Khan who sacked Baghdad in 1258, this Mongol ruler founded the Ilkhanate dynasty in Iran and established his capital at Tabriz and Maragheh.
STARS OVER MARAGHEH.expl_en: Hulagu embraced Persian culture and was persuaded by his astronomer vizier Nasir al-Din al-Tusi to construct the Maragheh Observatory in 1259.

STARS OVER MARAGHEH.clue_en: Serving as Ilkhanid vizier to Ghazan Khan, this Jewish convert physician wrote Jami al-Tawarikh (Compendium of Chronicles), the world's first true universal history.
STARS OVER MARAGHEH.expl_en: Rashid al-Din built the Rab'-e Rashidi academy complex in Tabriz, employing hundreds of scholars, paper makers, and calligraphers to copy his historical manuscripts.

STARS OVER MARAGHEH.clue_en: Founded in 1259 in Azerbaijan under Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, this astronomical observatory developed the 'Tusi-couple' geometrical model later utilized by Nicolaus Copernicus.
STARS OVER MARAGHEH.expl_en: Maragheh's 400,000-manuscript library and four-meter sextant produced the Zij-i Ilkhani planetary tables that circulated from China to Renaissance Italy.

STARS OVER MARAGHEH.clue_en: Reigning from Samarkand, this astronomer-prince and grandson of Timur accurately calculated the sidereal year to within 25 seconds of modern measurements before being assassinated by his son.
STARS OVER MARAGHEH.expl_en: Ulugh Beg's star catalogue Zij-i Sultani (1437) mapped 1,018 stars, honored today by a crater on the Moon bearing his name.

STARS OVER MARAGHEH.clue_en: Completed in 1430 for Timur's grandson Prince Baysunghur in Herat, this illustrated manuscript is universally revered as the supreme masterpiece of Persian miniature art.
STARS OVER MARAGHEH.expl_en: Inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register, its 21 surviving miniatures and calligraphy represent the zenith of the Timurid Herat School.

SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.clue_en: In March 1890, Nasir al-Din Shah granted this British major an exclusive 50-year worldwide monopoly over the production, sale, and export of all Iranian tobacco.
SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.expl_en: Talbot paid £15,000 in personal bribes to Prime Minister Amin al-Soltan and promised £15,000 annually to the Shah plus a quarter of net profits.

SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.clue_en: Living in exile in Samarra (Iraq), this supreme Marja-e Taqlid issued the historic December 1891 fatwa that made smoking water-pipes equivalent to war against the Hidden Imam.
SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.expl_en: The brief two-sentence fatwa spread by telegraph across Iran, uniting secular modernists, merchant guilds, and the clergy in the first successful mass civil disobedience movement.

SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.clue_en: Inside the royal palace harem, this favorite wife of Nasir al-Din Shah led his wives and concubines in smashing their crystal water-pipes (qalyan) in defiance of the sovereign.
SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.expl_en: When the Shah asked who had forbidden smoking in his own palace, Anis al-Dowleh famously answered: 'The same one who made me lawful (halal) unto you.'

SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.clue_en: This fiery pan-Islamic activist wrote an urgent letter to Mirza Shirazi from Basra in 1891 detailing the betrayal of Iranian sovereignty before being expelled from Iran.
SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.expl_en: Afghani had taken bast at Shah Abdol-Azim in 1890 before being dragged through snow by royal guards and dumped at the Ottoman frontier.

SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.ans_en: The First Foreign Loan (Imperial Bank Loan)
SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.clue_en: To cancel the Talbot concession in January 1892, the bankrupt Qajar state was forced to pay this enormous indemnity of £500,000, creating Iran's first foreign national debt.
opts_en: The First Foreign Loan (Imperial Bank Loan)
SMOKE 'EM IF YOU'VE GOT 'EM.expl_en: The British-owned Imperial Bank of Persia lent the funds at 6% interest, secured against the customs revenues of the Persian Gulf ports.

BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.clue_en: A close medical aide to Khomeini in Neauphle-le-Château, this American-educated cancer researcher served as Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister in the 1979 provisional government.
BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.expl_en: Yazdi and Bazargan met US National Security Advisor Zbigniew Brzezinski in Algiers on November 1, 1979, triggering the embassy takeover three days later.

BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.clue_en: Head of National Iranian Radio and Television and later Foreign Minister, this charismatic aide to Khomeini was executed by firing squad in Evin in 1982 for plotting to shell Jamaran.
BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.expl_en: Ghotbzadeh was implicated alongside Grand Ayatollah Shariatmadari in an army plot to assassinate Khomeini and bomb the clerical leadership in Jamaran.

BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.clue_en: Elected with 76% of the vote in January 1980, this Sorbonne economist wore simple civilian suits but was impeached by the Majles in June 1981 and disguised himself to flee to Paris.
BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.expl_en: Banisadr allied with Massoud Rajavi's MEK against the Islamic Republic Party; after his impeachment, the MEK launched a campaign of assassinations that killed hundreds of leaders.

BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.clue_en: Sprouting in mosques across every neighborhood in February 1979, these armed local revolutionary councils seized weapons, policed streets, and arrested former royalist officials.
BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.expl_en: Headed by Ayatollah Mahdavi Kani, the Komitehs of the Islamic Revolution functioned as autonomous neighborhood fiefdoms until merged into the Law Enforcement Force (NAJA) in 1991.

BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.clue_en: Serving as Secretary of the Revolutionary Council and later Majles Speaker and President, this pragmatist cleric from Rafsanjan was the central kingmaker of the new regime.
BAZARGAN'S BLUNT BLADE.expl_en: Rafsanjani survived an assassination attempt by the Forqan group in May 1979 and served as commander-in-chief of the war effort from 1988.

TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.clue_en: Following the October 1973 Arab-Israeli War, the Shah led OPEC at the Tehran meeting to quadruple oil prices from $3 to nearly this benchmark price per barrel.
TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.expl_en: Iran's petroleum revenues rocketed overnight from $5 billion in 1973 to over $20 billion in 1974, fueling the Shah's dream of creating the 'Great Civilization' (Tamaddon-e Bozorg).

TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.clue_en: Heading the Plan and Budget Organization, this Harvard-trained prince resigned after warning the Shah that pumping petrodollars into the economy would trigger runaway inflation.
TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.expl_en: At the August 1974 Ramsar conference, the Shah overruled economic planners and doubled the Fifth Plan budget, causing port congestion, cement shortages, and 30% inflation.

TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.clue_en: To combat soaring inflation in 1975, the Rastakhiz Party formed inspection squads that arrested over 20,000 shopkeepers and exiled 8,000 merchants under this controversial campaign.
TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.expl_en: University students were sent with police to seal bazaar stalls and jail prominent merchants like Habib Elghanian, destroying the centuries-old alliance between monarchy and bazaar.

TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.clue_en: During the petrodollar boom, this state-run automobile manufacturer produced hundreds of thousands of the Paykan, built under license from Britain's Hillman Hunter.
TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.expl_en: Founded by brothers Ahmad and Mahmoud Khayyami in 1962, Iran National made the Paykan ('Arrow') the ubiquitous national car of every Iranian family and taxi driver.

TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.clue_en: By 1976, foreign cargo ships had to wait up to six months in the Persian Gulf to unload goods, costing the Iranian government over $1 billion annually in this shipping penalty fee.
TWELVE DOLLARS A BARREL.expl_en: Over two hundred cargo vessels queued outside Khorramshahr and Bandar Abbas while goods rotted in hulls, exposing the massive infrastructure bottlenecks of the boom.

KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.clue_en: Appointed head of the Revolutionary Courts by Khomeini, this fiery cleric earned the moniker 'The Hanging Judge' for ordering hundreds of executions from the roof of Refah School.
KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.expl_en: Operating without defense attorneys or juries, Khalkhali executed over two hundred generals, ministers, and SAVAK officers in the first four months of the revolution.

KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.clue_en: The iron-fisted martial law governor of Tehran who ordered troops to stand fast on February 11, 1979, this lieutenant general gave a defiant military salute before his execution.
KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.expl_en: Rahimi shouted 'Javid Shah!' (Long Live the King) and saluted before the firing squad on the snowy roof of Refah School at midnight on February 15, 1979.

KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.clue_en: Before his execution in Evin in April 1979, former Prime Minister Hoveyda asked for a cigarette and warned the court: 'A system built on this kind of justice...'
KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.expl_en: Khalkhali shot Hoveyda in the neck during a recess to prevent Prime Minister Bazargan from obtaining a stay of execution from Khomeini in Qom.

KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.clue_en: Prominent Jewish philanthropist, plastics industrialist, and head of the Tehran Jewish community, his execution in May 1979 triggered the mass emigration of Iranian Jews.
KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.expl_en: Elghanian built the famous Plasco building in Tehran; his execution on charges of 'Zionism and corruption' prompted US Senator Jacob Javits to introduce the first Congressional sanctions.

KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.clue_en: Provisional Prime Minister Bazargan bitterly condemned the summary executions and secret trials in a famous television address, comparing the tribunals to this historical reign.
KHALKHALI'S GAVEL DROPS.expl_en: Bazargan decried that 'the revolution has given birth to Robespierres who chop off heads without due process of law.'

ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.clue_en: Housing the world's largest oil refinery on the Shatt al-Arab, this island city in Khuzestan became the flashpoint of the nationalization confrontation with Britain.
ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.expl_en: In October 1951, Mosaddegh expelled the last remaining British engineers from Abadan, who sailed down the Shatt al-Arab aboard the cruiser HMS Mauritius.

ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.clue_en: Known as the 'Soldier of Nationalization', this fiery orator and close lieutenant of Mosaddegh personally oversaw the seizure and unsealing of the Abadan refinery.
ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.expl_en: Makki rode atop oil tanks surrounded by thousands of cheering workers; his later defection from Mosaddegh was a major blow to the National Front.

ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.clue_en: In July 1952 (30 Tir), millions of Iranians took to the streets in defiance of royal tanks to demand the reinstatement of Mosaddegh following his dismissal by this premier.
ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.expl_en: Qavam issued a bombastic proclamation threatening to steer the ship of state with an iron hand, but resigned after four days of bloody street battles.

ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.ans_en: The International Court of Justice (The Hague)
ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.clue_en: Traveling to the Netherlands in June 1952, Dr. Mosaddegh personally addressed this international court, brilliantly arguing that the dispute was between Iran and a private company.
opts_en: The International Court of Justice (The Hague)
The European Court of Human Rights
ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.expl_en: By a vote of 9 to 5, the ICJ ruled in Iran's favor that it lacked jurisdiction because the 1933 concession was not an interstate treaty between governments.

ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.clue_en: In response to nationalization, the British Royal Navy imposed this severe naval embargo in the Persian Gulf, intercepting foreign tankers that attempted to purchase Iranian oil.
ABAPLAN GONE WRONG.expl_en: When the Italian tanker Rose Mary tried to export Iranian crude in 1952, British warships intercepted it and forced it into Aden, cutting Iran off from world oil markets.

THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.clue_en: In 1954, following the coup, military authorities uncovered a clandestine communist espionage network inside the armed forces comprising over 600 officers belonging to this party.
THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.expl_en: Twenty-seven military officers, including Colonel Siamak and Colonel Rouzbeh, were executed by firing squad, dismantling Soviet penetration of the Iranian officer corps.

THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.clue_en: Serving as chief of the CIA's Near East division and author of Countercoup, this grandson of an American president secretly entered Iran under the alias 'James Lockridge'.
THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.expl_en: Roosevelt operated out of a hidden cellar in the US Embassy compound, coordinating suitcase payments of $1 million in cash to royalist plotters and street gangs.

THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.clue_en: In 1958, this former Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces was arrested in a US-backed plot to overthrow Prime Minister Eqbal and curb the Shah's autocratic powers.
THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.expl_en: Gharani served three years in prison; after the 1979 Revolution, Khomeini appointed him the first Chief of the General Staff until assassinated by Forqan in April 1979.

THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.clue_en: British SIS intelligence operative who smuggled radio transmitters into Iran inside diplomatic pouches, he convinced the CIA to join Operation Boot.
THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.expl_en: Woodhouse famously framed the coup to the incoming Eisenhower administration not as protecting British oil profits, but as preventing a Soviet communist takeover of Iran.

THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.clue_en: Operating from 1959 to 1979, this joint US-Iranian secret eavesdropping installation in the northern mountains monitored Soviet telemetry and space missile tests at Baikonur.
THE SPY WHO LIKED KEBAB.expl_en: Listening posts at Kabkan and Behshahr near the Soviet border allowed the CIA to intercept telemetry from Soviet rocket launches until evacuated during the 1979 Revolution.

PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.clue_en: On April 18, 1988, the US Navy destroyed two Iranian oil platforms and sank the frigate Sahand in this largest surface naval battle fought by America since World War II.
PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.expl_en: Praying Mantis was launched in retaliation after the guided missile frigate USS Samuel B. Roberts struck an Iranian M-08 sea mine in international waters, nearly sinking.

PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.clue_en: On July 3, 1988, the guided-missile cruiser USS Vincennes shot down this civilian Iranian airliner over the Strait of Hormuz, killing all 290 passengers and crew aboard.
PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.expl_en: The Airbus A300 was climbing inside a designated commercial corridor on a flight from Bandar Abbas to Dubai when Captain Will Rogers III mistook it for an attacking F-14 Tomcat.

PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.ans_en: Reflagging under the US Flag (Operation Earnest Will)
PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.clue_en: In 1987, to protect Kuwaiti oil exports from Iranian sea mines and gunboat swarms, the United States placed eleven Kuwaiti tankers under this maritime arrangement.
opts_en: Reflagging under the US Flag (Operation Earnest Will)
PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.expl_en: On its maiden voyage under US Navy escort in July 1987, the reflagged supertanker Bridgeton struck an Iranian sea mine near Farsi Island, puncturing its outer hull.

PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.clue_en: Supplied by China and deployed on mobile launchers along the rugged coastline of the Strait of Hormuz, these anti-ship cruise missiles posed a lethal threat to Persian Gulf tankers.
PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.expl_en: With a 500-kilogram warhead and 100-kilometer range, Silkworm batteries at Kuhestak and Qeshm gave Iran the capability to choke commercial shipping in the strait.

PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.clue_en: The IRGC Navy deployed swarms of these small, high-speed armed motorboats to ambush commercial tankers and launch rocket-propelled grenades in hit-and-run attacks.
