PRAYING MANTIS ON PATROL.expl_en: Purchased from Sweden for coastal patrol, the 13-meter boats were mounted with 107mm multiple rocket launchers and DShK heavy machine guns by IRGC naval commandos.

BARBAD TO THE BONE.clue_en: Serving at the court of Sasanian King Khosrow II Parviz in the 7th century, this legendary court musician created the modal system of the Seven Royal Modes (Khosravani).
BARBAD TO THE BONE.expl_en: Nezami's Khosrow and Shirin describes musical duels between Barbad and the harpist Nakisa, immortalizing Barbad as the father of Persian art music.

BARBAD TO THE BONE.clue_en: Celebrated for his velvet baritone and iconic black-rimmed glasses, this mid-century vocalist immortalized the patriotic anthem Ey Iran and the tragic ballad Elaheh-ye Naz.
BARBAD TO THE BONE.expl_en: Banan was the premier vocalist of Davood Pirnia's prestigious Golha (Flowers of Persian Song and Music) radio programs broadcast nationwide from 1956 to 1979.

BARBAD TO THE BONE.clue_en: This virtuoso Setar master and scholar popularized the instrument in the 1980s with his bestselling album Gol-e Sadbarg (One Hundred-Petaled Rose), featuring vocalist Shahram Nazeri.
BARBAD TO THE BONE.expl_en: Gol-e Sadbarg commemorated the 800th anniversary of Rumi; it became the bestselling classical instrumental album in Iranian recording history.

BARBAD TO THE BONE.clue_en: Composed by Hossein Alizadeh in 1983 for ney and Western string orchestra during the darkest days of the war, this poignant concerto is titled after the reed flute.
BARBAD TO THE BONE.expl_en: Featuring Jamshid Andalibi on ney, NeyNava (Song of the Reed / Plain of Nineveh) became the grief-stricken soundtrack to the tragedy and resilience of the 1980s.

BARBAD TO THE BONE.clue_en: Born in 1845, this court master of the tar and setar organized and codified the disparate vocal and instrumental melodies of Persian music into the canonical Radif.
BARBAD TO THE BONE.expl_en: Mirza Abdollah's home was a musical academy; his students included Darvish Khan, Esma'il Mehdi-Qoli, and his own sons Ahmad Ebadi and Javad Ebadi.

WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.clue_en: In 2014, this Harvard-trained geometer and Stanford professor became the first woman and first Iranian ever to win the Fields Medal, the 'Nobel Prize of Mathematics'.
WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.expl_en: Mirzakhani made groundbreaking contributions to the dynamics and geometry of Riemann surfaces; her birthday, May 12, is recognized internationally as Women in Mathematics Day.

WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.clue_en: Appointed Iran's first female presiding judge in 1969, this human rights attorney was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2003 for her defense of children and political dissidents.
WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.expl_en: Ebadi was demoted to a court clerk after the 1979 revolution because clerical jurists held that women were too emotional to serve as judges; she later founded the Defenders of Human Rights Center.

WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.clue_en: Starring in The Downpour (1972) and Bashu, the Little Stranger (1986), this magnetic stage and screen actress emigrated to Sweden, becoming a leading actress of the Royal Dramatic Theatre.
WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.expl_en: Taslimi's fiercely independent performances under director Bahram Beyzai defined the golden era of modern Iranian auteur cinema.

WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.clue_en: Known as 'Dabagh', this revolutionary militant fought in Lebanon alongside Chamran, guarded Khomeini in Paris, and was appointed the first female commander of the IRGC in Hamadan.
WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.expl_en: Dabagh was one of three envoys chosen by Khomeini in January 1989 to travel to Moscow to deliver his historic philosophical letter to Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev.

WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.clue_en: In September 2006, this Iranian-American engineer and entrepreneur made history as the first female private space explorer and first Iranian in space, docking at the ISS.
WOMEN WHO MOVED THE REALM.expl_en: Ansari wore the Iranian and American flags on her spacesuit and performed experiments on cell biology aboard the Soyuz TMA-9 flight.

CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.clue_en: Set in besieged Abadan, this acclaimed 2005 novel by Habib Ahmadzadeh follows an 18-year-old artillery spotter engaged in a psychological duel against Iraqi radar.
CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.expl_en: The 'Doomsday Machine' was a British-supplied Cymbeline mortar-locating radar deployed by Iraqi forces to obliterate Iranian artillery batteries.

CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.clue_en: Authored by Ahmad Dehqan, this unvarnished combat novel broke with official propaganda to depict the grim terror, thirst, and gore endured during Operation Karbala-5.
CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.expl_en: Translated into English by Paul Sprachman, the novel won the twenty-year Sacred Defense literary prize for its unromanticized realism.

CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.clue_en: A construction worker from Mashhad who commanded the 18th Javad ol-A'emmeh Brigade, this illiterate mystic-warrior was immortalized in the million-copy bestseller Khak-haye Narm-e Koushk.
CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.expl_en: Authored by Sa'id Owhadi, Khak-haye Narm-e Koushk (The Soft Soil of Koushk) recounts Borunsi's visions of Lady Fatima guiding his platoon through minefields before his death in 1985.

CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.clue_en: This desolate desert battlefield in Ilam and Khuzestan became known as the 'Graveyard of Tanks', where thousands of young Basij volunteers cleared minefields with their bodies.
CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.expl_en: Documentary filmmaker Morteza Avini was martyred in Fakkeh on April 9, 1993, while filming unexploded ordnance for Chronicles of Victory.

CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.clue_en: Commander of the 31st Ashura Division from Tabriz, this beloved hero was killed in a boat on the Tigris during Operation Badr in 1985, his body hit by an RPG and lost to the waters.
CHESS WITH DOOMSDAY MACHINES.expl_en: When his brother Ali was killed hours earlier, Bakeri refused to evacuate his body before ordinary soldiers; his life inspired the 2022 film The Situation of Mehdi (Mogheiat-e Mehdi).

NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.clue_en: These iconic architectural cooling chimneys rising above Yazd desert rooftops capture desert breezes and funnel chilled air down into interior living quarters.
NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.expl_en: The tallest windcatcher in the world stands 33 meters high in the Dowlatabad Garden of Yazd.

NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.clue_en: Stretching for thousands of kilometers beneath the desert plateau, this ancient UNESCO-listed system of subterranean gently sloping water channels sustained Persian oasis cities.
NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.expl_en: Invented in Iran in the early 1st millennium BC, qanats rely entirely on gravity to bring mountain aquifer water to dry plains without evaporation.

NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.clue_en: Perched on barren hills outside Yazd, these circular stone towers were used by Zoroastrians for ritual excarnation until the mid-20th century.
NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.expl_en: Zoroastrians placed bodies on Dakhmeh towers to be consumed by birds of prey, avoiding polluting the sacred elements of earth and fire.

NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.clue_en: Housed in the Atashkadeh of Yazd, this sacred Zoroastrian flame of the highest grade (Atash Bahram) has been burning continuously since this century AD.
NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.expl_en: The sacred fire was kept burning in secret caves near Ardakan before being moved to the Yazd Fire Temple in 1934.

NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.clue_en: Tucked into a sheer mountain cliff near Yazd, this holy pilgrimage site commemorates Nikbanou, daughter of the last Sasanian king Yazdegerd III.
NOT IN MY BACK-YAZD.expl_en: According to legend, the mountain opened to shelter the Sasanian princess from invaders, and the dripping water represents the mountain weeping for her.

KHORASAN-WICH.clue_en: Producing over ninety percent of the world's supply of this 'red gold', the fields of southern Khorasan harvest the delicate red stigmas of this crocus flower.
KHORASAN-WICH.expl_en: It takes over 150,000 hand-picked crocus flowers to produce a single kilogram of dried Persian saffron.

KHORASAN-WICH.clue_en: Mined for over 3,000 years in the Madan hills northwest of Nishapur, these sky-blue gemstones were traded along the Silk Road to pharaohs and emperors.
KHORASAN-WICH.expl_en: Nishapur turquoise was the global gold standard for robin's egg blue stones, worn by kings as protective talismans against poison and evil.

KHORASAN-WICH.clue_en: In Tus near Mashhad, this 1934 cubic white marble mausoleum inspired by Achaemenid architecture honors the composer of the Shahnameh.
KHORASAN-WICH.expl_en: Designed by Karim Taherzadeh Behzad, the mausoleum is inscribed with scenes from Rostam's battles hewn in stone bas-relief.

KHORASAN-WICH.clue_en: This fortified natural plateau in Khorasan surrounded by sheer cliff walls served as Nader Shah's impenetrable mountain treasure fortress.
KHORASAN-WICH.expl_en: Within Kalat, Nader built the Sun Palace (Kakh-e Khorshid) with fluted circular towers to store the treasures looted from Delhi.

KHORASAN-WICH.clue_en: Designed by architect Houshang Seyhoun in 1963, this soaring 22-meter open concrete rhombic structure covers the tomb of the poet-mathematician in Nishapur.
KHORASAN-WICH.expl_en: Seyhoun integrated Khayyam's three aspects—astronomer, mathematician, and poet—by building ten intersecting concrete petals adorned with Persian quatrains.

WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.clue_en: Rising 25 meters above the Khuzestan plains near Susa, this massive 13th-century BC baked-brick temple tower is the best-preserved ziggurat in the world.
WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.expl_en: Built around 1250 BC by King Untash-Napirisha to honor the god Inshushinak, Chogha Zanbil was Iran's first UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979.

WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.clue_en: King of Elam who built Chogha Zanbil and dedicated its inner sanctum to the bull-god Inshushinak was named this.
WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.expl_en: Untash-Napirisha founded the ceremonial city of Dur-Untash, bringing together Highland and Lowland Elamite pantheons.

WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.clue_en: In the 12th century BC, Elamite king Shutruk-Nakhkhunte raided Babylon and carried off this monumental diorite law stele as war booty to Susa.
WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.expl_en: French archaeologist Jacques de Morgan discovered the Code of Hammurabi at Susa in 1901, where it was shipped to the Louvre Museum.

WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.clue_en: In 647 BC, this ruthless Neo-Assyrian emperor sacked Susa, famously salting the earth and boasting that he had turned Elam into a wasteland.
WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.expl_en: Ashurbanipal's stone reliefs in Nineveh depict Elamite prisoners forced to grind the bones of their ancestors before execution.

WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.clue_en: In 2020, French archaeologist François Desset announced the decipherment of this ancient 4,000-year-old writing system used in southern Iran.
WE'VE GOT ELAM-ENTARY EVIDENCE.expl_en: Linear Elamite was a purely phonetic syllabic script used in the late 3rd millennium BC, proven to record the Elamite language.

KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.clue_en: According to Herodotus, this wise village judge was elected the first king of the united Medes around 700 BC, establishing the capital at Ecbatana.
KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.expl_en: Herodotus wrote that Deioces built Ecbatana with seven concentric colored circular walls, living secluded in the central citadel.

KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.clue_en: In 612 BC, this Median warrior king formed an alliance with Nabopolassar of Babylon to storm and level Nineveh, annihilating the Assyrian Empire.
KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.expl_en: Cyaxares reorganized Median armed forces into distinct archer, spearmen, and cavalry regiments, creating a professional army.

KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.clue_en: Modern city in the Zagros Mountains that sits atop the ancient Median capital Ecbatana (Hagmatana / Place of Gathering).
KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.expl_en: Ecbatana served as the summer capital of Achaemenid, Parthian, and Sasanian monarchs seeking refuge from Mesopotamian heat.

KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.ans_en: Battle of the Eclipse (Battle of the Halys)
KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.clue_en: The solar eclipse of May 28, 585 BC, accurately predicted by Thales of Miletus, halted this decisive battle between Cyaxares and the Lydians.
opts_en: Battle of the Eclipse (Battle of the Halys)
KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.expl_en: Both kings were terrified by day turning to night, immediately laying down weapons and sealing peace with royal dynastic marriages.

KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.clue_en: Excavated near Malayer in Hamadan, this Iron Age hill citadel site features the oldest surviving Zoroastrian fire temple tower in the world.
KINGS OF THE MEDES & BOUNDS.expl_en: Tepe Nush-i Jan contains an 8th-century BC central fire altar room with preserved mudbrick arched roofs carefully buried in shale before being abandoned.

SEALED WITH A DISS.clue_en: Issued by Mozaffar al-Din Shah on August 5, 1906, this royal decree consented to the creation of a national consultative assembly (Majles).
SEALED WITH A DISS.expl_en: Signed by the dying Shah on his sickbed, it ordered the convening of an assembly of all estates to draft the fundamental law of the empire.

SEALED WITH A DISS.clue_en: In 1807, Napoleon Bonaparte signed this military alliance treaty with Fath-Ali Shah at a Prussian castle, promising to help Iran recover Georgia from Russia.
SEALED WITH A DISS.expl_en: Napoleon dispatched General Claude Mathieu de Gardane with 70 French military engineers to modernize the Iranian army before abandoning the alliance.

SEALED WITH A DISS.clue_en: Carved into jade, carnelian, or ruby and dipped in black soot ink, this calligraphic signet seal was pressed onto royal letters by Iranian monarchs in place of a signature.
SEALED WITH A DISS.expl_en: The keeper of the royal seal (Mohrdar-e Saltanati) held immense power, stamping imperial firmans with the Shah's personal gem.

SEALED WITH A DISS.clue_en: In 1873, Nasir al-Din Shah became the first Iranian monarch to visit Europe, keeping an intimate diary describing his reception by this British Queen.
SEALED WITH A DISS.expl_en: Victoria invested Nasir al-Din Shah with the Order of the Garter at Windsor Castle, though royal courtiers were baffled by Persian dining etiquette.

SEALED WITH A DISS.clue_en: During the Tobacco Protests of 1891, thousands of Iranian merchants and scholars took refuge from royal arrest inside this inviolable sanctuary space.
SEALED WITH A DISS.expl_en: Traditional sites of Bast included holy shrines (Shah Abdol-Azim, Fatima Masumeh), royal stables, and the telegraph offices of the Indo-European line.

HORSING AROUND IN NISA.clue_en: Carved from elephant tusks and excavated at Old Nisa, these magnificent drinking horns with winged beast terminals are known by this Greek-derived term.
HORSING AROUND IN NISA.expl_en: Over forty ivory rhytons were found in the royal treasure house of Nisa, blending Greek Hellenistic carving with Persian gryphon and lion motifs.

HORSING AROUND IN NISA.clue_en: Armored head-to-toe in overlapping iron or bronze scale mail and riding armored Nisean warhorses, these heavy Parthian shock cavalry were called this.
HORSING AROUND IN NISA.expl_en: Cataphracts wielded a four-meter two-handed heavy lance (Kontos) capable of impaling two Roman legionaries at once.

HORSING AROUND IN NISA.clue_en: The founder of the Arsacid Parthian dynasty, a Parni chieftain who rebelled against the Seleucid satrap Andragoras around 247 BC, was named this.
HORSING AROUND IN NISA.expl_en: All subsequent thirty-one Parthian monarchs took the throne name 'Arsaces' (Ashk) on their official coinage to honor the dynastic founder.

HORSING AROUND IN NISA.clue_en: In 141 BC, this Parthian conqueror captured Seleucia-on-the-Tigris and Babylon, driving the Hellenistic Greeks out of the Iranian plateau.
HORSING AROUND IN NISA.expl_en: Mithridates captured the Seleucid king Demetrius II Nicator alive, treating him honorably and giving him a Parthian princess in marriage.

HORSING AROUND IN NISA.clue_en: The bronze statue of a tall Parthian nobleman wearing belted tunic and wide trousers with a dagger at his hip was unearthed at this Khuzestan site.
HORSING AROUND IN NISA.expl_en: Now in the National Museum of Iran, the 1.94-meter hollow-cast bronze statue is humanity's most striking portrait of an ancient Parthian grandee.

SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.clue_en: Commissioned by Nasir al-Din Shah in 1869 to locate unset gems, this 66-centimeter golden sphere is encrusted with over 51,000 diamonds, rubies, and emeralds.
SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.expl_en: The oceans are crafted from emeralds, Iran and Britain in diamonds, and southern Africa in rubies in the Central Bank vault.

SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.clue_en: Weighing 182 carats and possessing an exceedingly rare pale pink tint, this table-cut diamond is the largest uncut pink diamond in the world.
SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.expl_en: Nader Shah brought the Daria-i-Noor from the Mughal treasury in Delhi in 1739.

SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.clue_en: Designed by French architect André Godard in 1937, the entrance facade of the National Museum of Iran in Tehran is modeled on this Sasanian arch.
SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.expl_en: Godard used red Roman-sized fired bricks to evoke Sasanian imperial majesty for the Museum of Ancient Iran (Muzeh-ye Iran-e Bastan).

SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.clue_en: Constructed for the 1926 coronation of Reza Shah, the Pahlavi Crown is topped by a plume of white egret feathers and encrusted with this many diamonds.
SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.expl_en: The crown features a massive 60-carat yellow diamond in the center of its sunburst, fabricated by master Caucasian jeweler Serajeddin.

SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.clue_en: Worn by Qajar monarchs from Fath-Ali Shah to Ahmad Shah, this tall velvet crown encrusted with 1,800 pearls and a giant spinel is known by this name.
SHAH-PING FOR ANTIQUES.expl_en: Taj-e Kiani was named after the mythical Kayanian kings of the Shahnameh, draped in red velvet and pearls.

DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.clue_en: Rising 5,609 meters above sea level in the Alborz range, this dormant stratovolcano is the highest peak in Iran and the highest volcano in Asia.
DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.expl_en: Damavand features year-round summit glaciers, active sulfur fumaroles near its crater, and is celebrated in Bahar's ode 'O white demon with chained feet'.

DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.clue_en: According to Persian legend, this heroic archer climbed Mount Damavand to loose an arrow that flew for three days, establishing the boundary between Iran and Turan.
DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.expl_en: Siavash Kasra'i's 1959 modern epic poem Arash-e Kamangir made the archer an enduring symbol of self-sacrificing patriotic martyrdom.

DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.clue_en: In the Shahnameh, the tyrant Zahhak, with flesh-eating serpents sprouting from his shoulders, was captured by Fereydun and chained in a cave beneath this peak.
DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.expl_en: Legend holds that sulfur fumes and earthquakes emanating from Damavand are the fiery breathing and thrashing of the chained tyrant Zahhak.

DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.clue_en: Flowing through a dramatic gorge carved into the Alborz along the foot of Damavand, this river empties into the Caspian Sea near Babolsar.
DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.expl_en: The Haraz Road (Road 77) carved along the canyon walls is one of the most treacherous and spectacular mountain highways in the world.

DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.clue_en: Located on the southern slopes of Damavand, this alpine national park is famous for wild scarlet poppy fields blooming each spring against snowy peaks.
DAMAVAND-ING RESPECT.expl_en: Lar Dam reservoirs provide drinking water to Tehran, surrounded by meadows hosting rare endemic brown trout (Qezel-ala).

POETS IN EXILE.clue_en: A master of imagist modern verse, this poet fled to Los Angeles after 1979, famously longing for Tehran in poems like Collyrium of the Sun.
POETS IN EXILE.expl_en: Naderpour lived in California until his death in 2000, his gravestone inscribed with his famous poem 'My sorrow is an ancient forest.'

POETS IN EXILE.clue_en: Co-author of The Cow and leading dramatist, this medical doctor fled into French exile where he drank himself to death, buried in Père Lachaise near Sadegh Hedayat.
POETS IN EXILE.expl_en: Writing under the pseudonym Gowhar Morad, Sa'edi died of gastrointestinal bleeding in Paris in 1985.

POETS IN EXILE.clue_en: Living in East Berlin for four decades after the 1953 coup, this author of Her Eyes taught Persian literature at Humboldt University.
POETS IN EXILE.expl_en: Alavi returned briefly to Iran after the 1979 revolution, but returned to Berlin where he died in 1997.

POETS IN EXILE.clue_en: This brilliant satirist and diplomat penned the comic masterpiece My Uncle Napoleon (Da'i Jan Napoleon) in Geneva and Paris exile.
POETS IN EXILE.expl_en: My Uncle Napoleon satirized the widespread Iranian paranoia of British conspiracy, adapted into a record-shattering 1976 television series by Nasser Taghvai.

POETS IN EXILE.clue_en: Author of the feminist novella Women Without Men (Zanan bedun-e Mardan), this woman was repeatedly jailed in the 1980s before settling in the US.
POETS IN EXILE.expl_en: Her book was adapted into a Venice Silver Lion-winning film by Shirin Neshat in 2009.

THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.clue_en: Baked on a sloping bed of burning river pebbles in giant dome ovens, this whole wheat sourdough flatbread is considered the king of traditional Iranian breads.
THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.expl_en: Sangak ('little pebbles') was historically invented for Persian armies on the march, where soldiers carried river stones to build portable ovens.

THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.clue_en: Brought to Tehran in the late 19th century by Hazara and Khorasani immigrants, this thick oval crusty bread glazed with baking soda wash is named after this ethnic group.
THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.expl_en: Barbari refers to the Hazara community of eastern Khorasan who originally operated the bakeries in southern Tehran.

THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.clue_en: In December 1942, grain hoarding and Allied requisitioning caused starving crowds to storm the Majles and riot over bread in this capital city.
THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.expl_en: Protesters looted Prime Minister Qavam's private residence after discovering sawdust and pebbles baked into municipal loaves.

THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.clue_en: Introduced in 1980 during the Iran-Iraq War, this system of colored ration coupons for meat, sugar, rice, and cooking oil was known by this French loanword.
THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.expl_en: Kupon-e bazi (coupon trading) created a parallel black market economy that sustained working-class families throughout the eight-year war.

THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.clue_en: To keep food prices artificially low in the 1970s, the Pahlavi state created this giant consumer cooperative agency with subsidized supermarkets across Iran.
THE BREAD & BUTTER OF POLITICS.expl_en: Koorosh department stores were targeted for nationalization in 1979 and renamed Forushgah-e Qods.

A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.clue_en: Engineered through solid mountain rock by Austrian and local workers in the 1930s, this winding scenic highway links Karaj to the Caspian port of Chaloos.
A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.expl_en: The 1,884-meter Kandovan Tunnel, hand-chiseled through the Alborz mountain crest in 1938, cut travel time from Tehran to the Caspian from days to hours.

A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.clue_en: In 1962, brothers Ahmad and Mahmoud Khayyami founded this premier industrial giant to assemble the Paykan under license from Britain's Rootes Group.
A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.expl_en: Between 1967 and 2005, over two million Paykans were manufactured, becoming the ubiquitous chariot of Iranian middle-class life.

A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.clue_en: In 1900, this monarch purchased Iran's first two automobiles—twin open-top French Gardner-Serpollet steam carriages—during his tour of Belgium and Paris.
A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.expl_en: One car broke down en route through the Caucasus mountains; the surviving carriage was driven in Tehran by French chauffeur Monsieur Varelet.

A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.clue_en: The British Rootes Group vehicle that served as the chassis and mechanical design base for the Iranian Paykan was known by this model name in the UK.
A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.expl_en: The 1725cc four-cylinder engine and sturdy leaf-spring rear suspension were uniquely suited to rough Iranian provincial roads.

A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.clue_en: Located in northern Tehran, this former imperial estate houses the Royal Automobile Museum exhibiting bulletproof Rolls-Royces, Mercedes 600s, and Ferraris.
A ROLLS-ROYCE FOR REZA.expl_en: The museum features an extraordinary bespoke electric Panther De Ville, gifts from international monarchs, and the Shah's personal Porsche 911.

TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.clue_en: Revered as the Robin Hood of the Caspian forests, this bearded cleric established the anti-imperialist Jangal (Forest) guerrilla movement in 1915.
TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.expl_en: Mirza Kuchik Khan proclaimed the Soviet Republic of Gilan in Rasht in June 1920 with Red Army support.

TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.clue_en: In June 1920, Bolshevik naval vessels landed at this Caspian port, driving out British forces and establishing the Persian Socialist Soviet Republic.
TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.expl_en: Admiral Fyodor Raskolnikov led the Caspian Flotilla that shelled British forces withdrawing down the Manjil road to Qazvin.

TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.clue_en: Harvested from the beluga sturgeon native to the southern Caspian Sea, this black roe was world-renowned as Iran's most luxurious culinary export.
TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.expl_en: Under the Qajars, Russian industrialist Stepan Lianozov held the exclusive concession over Caspian fisheries (Shilat).

TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.clue_en: Introduced by Kashef al-Saltaneh who smuggled seedlings out of British India in his walking stick in 1899, this crop blankets the hills of Lahijan.
TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.expl_en: Mohammad Mirza Kashef al-Saltaneh is commemorated as the 'Father of Iranian Tea' at the National Tea Museum in Lahijan.

TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.clue_en: This fairytale terraced village in Gilan features mud-straw houses built into the mountainside where the roof of one house serves as the courtyard of the house above.
TALES FROM THE CASPIAN SHORE.expl_en: Masuleh's unique interconnected architecture forbids all motor vehicles, creating an idyllic car-free pedestrian village.

PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.clue_en: Designed in 1961 by 22-year-old art student Edward Zohrabian, the iconic logo of Iran Air depicts this mythical Persian griffin-bird found at Persepolis.
PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.expl_en: Homa (the mythical bird of good fortune that bestows sovereignty upon whose head it casts a shadow) was acclaimed by IATA as one of the world's most beautiful airline logos.

PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.clue_en: In the mid-1970s, Iran Air was the first international airline to operate this specialized ultra-long-range Boeing aircraft nonstop between Tehran and New York.
PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.expl_en: The Boeing 747SP ('Special Performance') featured a shortened fuselage and taller tail fin, allowing Iran Air to complete the 6,336-mile trans-Atlantic flight in 11 hours.

PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.clue_en: Designed by architect Iraj Moshiri, this main international airport of Tehran served as Iran's primary aviation gateway from 1958 until commercial long-haul flights moved south.
PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.expl_en: Mehrabad's modernist concrete passenger terminal was celebrated for its dramatic sweeping roofline and views of snowy Mount Damavand.

PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.clue_en: Commander of the Imperial Iranian Air Force's Golden Crown aerobatic team and head of physical education, this charismatic general was executed on the Refah School roof in 1979.
PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.expl_en: Known as the 'Blue-Eyed General', Jahanbani reportedly refused a blindfold before the firing squad, declaring: 'I am proud of my service to Iranian aviation.'

PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.clue_en: On February 1, 1979, Ayatollah Khomeini returned to Tehran from sixteen years of exile aboard a chartered Boeing 747 operated by this national airline.
PERSIAN FLIGHTS OF FANCY.expl_en: Aboard the flight, ABC News correspondent Peter Jennings asked Khomeini what he felt returning to Iran after so long, to which he famously answered: 'Nothing' (Hichi).

THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.clue_en: In the First Labor of the Haft Khan, Rostam was asleep when his faithful warhorse Rakhsh fought and trampled this ferocious predator to death.
THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.expl_en: Rostam chided Rakhsh for risking his life alone, warning him: 'If you had been slain, who would have carried my heavy armor into Mazandaran?'

THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.clue_en: In the Second Labor, dying of dehydration in the scorching desert sands, Rostam prayed to God and was miraculously guided to a water spring by this animal.
THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.expl_en: Rostam praised the Creator for sending the divine ram, quenching his and Rakhsh's thirst before facing the fire-breathing dragon.

THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.clue_en: In the Fourth Labor, Rostam sat beside an enchanted stream and sang of his sorrows until this enchantress approached disguised as a beautiful damsel.
THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.expl_en: When Rostam handed her a goblet of wine and uttered the name of God, the illusion broke and her true black demonic form was revealed, whereupon Rostam lassooed and cleaved her in two.

THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.clue_en: In the Fifth Labor, Rostam captured this local border chieftain, promising to make him King of Mazandaran if he guided him through the dark enchantments.
THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.expl_en: Bound with a leather lariat, Oulad faithfully guided Rostam past the bottomless pits and scorching winds to the cavern of the White Demon.

THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.clue_en: In the Sixth Labor, Rostam decapitated this demonic champion outside his fortress, throwing his army into panic.
THE SEVEN LABORS OF ROSTAM.expl_en: Rostam charged Arzhang's camp shouting like thunder, tore off his head with his bare hands, and hurled it into the ranks of the Mazandaran demons.

CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.clue_en: Regarded as the 'Bride of Islamic Calligraphic Scripts', this flowing, cursive Persian script was invented in the 14th century by Mir Ali Tabrizi.
CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.expl_en: Nastaliq combines Naskh and Ta'liq, inspired according to legend by the graceful curves of flying geese.

CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.clue_en: Serving at the court of Shah Abbas I in Isfahan, this supreme calligrapher was murdered in 1615 by jealous courtiers, his style remaining the benchmark of Nastaliq.
CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.expl_en: Mir Emad's individual calligraphic folios (Qet'eh) were traded across India, the Ottoman Empire, and Europe for their weight in gold.

CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.clue_en: Invented in the 17th century for fast administrative court correspondence, this ornate broken script was perfected by Darvish Abdol-Majid Taleqani.
CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.expl_en: Shekasteh linked letters that were traditionally unjoined, creating dynamic visual rhythms resembling swaying branches.

CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.clue_en: Persian scribes crafted luxury carrying cases for their reed pens and inkwells using lacquered papier-mâché painted with nightingales and roses, known by this name.
CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.expl_en: Qalamdans were sliding wooden or papier-mâché sleeves tucked into a scribe's belt sash, painted by master Qajar miniaturists.

CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.clue_en: The finest reed pens (Qalam-e Ney) used by Iranian calligraphers are harvested from the dense river reed-beds of this southern Khuzestan city.
CALLIGRAPHY & INKWELLS.expl_en: Dezful reeds are seasoned for months until they turn glossy dark brown and ring like porcelain when struck.

THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.clue_en: In May 1974, French hematologists Georges Flandrin and Jean Bernard secretly diagnosed the Shah with this rare cancer of the lymphatic system.
THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.expl_en: The Shah demanded complete secrecy; even Empress Farah Diba was kept in the dark about the fatal diagnosis until autumn 1978.

THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.clue_en: To conceal his treatments from the CIA and Iranian public, French doctors flew into Tehran on commercial flights carrying drugs labeled under this cover name.
THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.expl_en: The Shah feared showing physical weakness would encourage Khomeini and cause Washington to seek an alternative leader.

THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.clue_en: In October 1979, President Jimmy Carter reluctantly allowed the exiled Shah into the United States for emergency medical treatment at this hospital.
THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.expl_en: Admitted under the alias 'David D. Newsom', the Shah's presence in New York provoked the storming of the US Embassy in Tehran two weeks later.

THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.clue_en: After being expelled from the United States and Panama, the dying Shah was granted unconditional royal asylum in Cairo by this Egyptian President.
THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.expl_en: Sadat declared: 'The Shah helped Egypt when we were alone; I will not abandon him when the world turns its back.'

THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.clue_en: Famed Houston heart surgeon who flew to Cairo in March 1980 to perform a splenectomy on the Shah was named this.
THE SHAHS SECRET ILLNESS.expl_en: DeBakey removed the Shah's massive 3.5-kilogram leukemic spleen at Maadi Military Hospital in Cairo.

AYAT-ALL-THAT.clue_en: In his 1970 Najaf lectures, Ayatollah Khomeini articulated this radical political doctrine asserting that the supreme Islamic jurist must rule the state directly.
AYAT-ALL-THAT.expl_en: Published as Islamic Government: Governance of the Jurist, it broke with centuries of quietist Shi'i theology awaiting the return of the Hidden Imam.

AYAT-ALL-THAT.clue_en: The traditional Shi'i legal school that championed rational deduction (Ijtihad) over literal scriptural traditions in the 18th century is known as this.
AYAT-ALL-THAT.expl_en: Led by Vahid Behbahani in Karbala, the Usuli victory established the absolute authority of living Mujtahids over the faithful.

AYAT-ALL-THAT.clue_en: The Shi'i religious tax of one-fifth levied on annual surplus wealth, channeled directly to Grand Ayatollahs to fund seminaries and stipends, is this.
AYAT-ALL-THAT.expl_en: Khums is divided into Sahm-e Imam (Share of the Imam) and Sahm-e Sadat (Share of the Prophet's descendants), giving the Hawza financial independence from the state.

AYAT-ALL-THAT.clue_en: To attain the rank of Ayatollah and Marja-e Taqlid, a scholar must be granted this formal diploma certifying their mastery of independent legal derivation.
AYAT-ALL-THAT.expl_en: Granted by senior masters in Najaf or Qom, an Ijaza certifies that the scholar possesses the capacity to deduce original Islamic rulings from the Quran and Sunnah.

AYAT-ALL-THAT.clue_en: The manual of Islamic jurisprudence published by every Grand Ayatollah as a practical guide for their followers is known by this Arabic title.
AYAT-ALL-THAT.expl_en: The Risalah details rulings on prayer, fasting, business transactions, and purity, required reading for every practicing Shi'i follower (Muqallid).

SHAH-ME ON YOU.clue_en: The Shah's formidable twin sister who was nicknamed 'The Black Panther' by French journalists for her political assertiveness was named this.
SHAH-ME ON YOU.expl_en: Ashraf met secretly with Kermit Roosevelt and General Norman Schwarzkopf Sr. in Paris in 1953 to convince her hesitant brother to back the coup against Mosaddegh.

SHAH-ME ON YOU.clue_en: Appointed Empress (Shahbanu) in 1967 and designated regent in case of the Shah's death, this third wife of the Shah was a patron of modern art and architecture.
SHAH-ME ON YOU.expl_en: Farah Diba established the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art in 1977, acquiring masterpieces by Picasso, Warhol, Rothko, and Pollock.

SHAH-ME ON YOU.clue_en: The Shah's exclusive winter retreat in the Swiss Alps, where he skied and conducted informal foreign diplomacy each January, was located in this luxury resort.
SHAH-ME ON YOU.expl_en: The Shah's month-long vacations at Villa Suvretta with kingpins and foreign journalists were heavily criticized during domestic economic crises.

SHAH-ME ON YOU.clue_en: The elite 4,000-man bodyguard division tasked with protecting the royal family, who swore personal blood oaths to the Shah, was known as this.
SHAH-ME ON YOU.expl_en: Named after the ancient 10,000 Achaemenid Immortals, all candidates had to exceed six feet in height and undergo rigorous ideological screening.

SHAH-ME ON YOU.clue_en: Between 1931 and 1936, the young Crown Prince Mohammad Reza was sent by his father to attend this prestigious Swiss boarding school near Lake Geneva.
SHAH-ME ON YOU.expl_en: At Le Rosey, the future Shah befriended Western classmates like Prince Rainier of Monaco, developing fluent French and a lifelong passion for tennis and skiing.

OPEC AND DOWN.clue_en: Founded in Baghdad in September 1960, Iran was one of the five founding members of OPEC alongside Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and this South American nation.
OPEC AND DOWN.expl_en: Venezuelan oil minister Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo and Iranian delegates forged the cartel to counter unilateral price cuts by the 'Seven Sisters' Western oil majors.

OPEC AND DOWN.clue_en: Iran's chief OPEC representative who negotiated the historic 1973 price hikes and was later taken hostage by Carlos the Jackal in Vienna in 1975 was named this.
OPEC AND DOWN.expl_en: Amouzegar was held at gunpoint in Vienna alongside Saudi oil minister Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani before being ransomed and flown to Algiers.

OPEC AND DOWN.clue_en: On December 21, 1975, this Venezuelan Marxist terrorist stormed the OPEC ministerial conference in Vienna, taking 63 hostages including eleven oil ministers.
OPEC AND DOWN.expl_en: Carlos demanded the assassination of Yamani and Amouzegar, but was paid an estimated $20 to $50 million in ransom by Arab governments to release them in Algiers.

OPEC AND DOWN.clue_en: In 1986, during the Iran-Iraq War, Saudi Arabia flooded the global market with cheap oil to punish Iran, causing crude prices to crash to this historic low per barrel.
OPEC AND DOWN.expl_en: The price crash choked off Iran's foreign exchange earnings, making it impossible to purchase modern weapons and forcing Khomeini to accept UN Resolution 598 in 1988.

OPEC AND DOWN.clue_en: Headquartered initially in Geneva from 1960 to 1965, OPEC relocated its permanent global secretariat to this neutral European capital city.
OPEC AND DOWN.expl_en: Austrian Chancellor Bruno Kreisky granted OPEC full extraterritorial diplomatic status in Vienna along the Danube Canal.

THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.clue_en: On June 23, 1908, this Tsarist Russian commander of the Persian Cossack Brigade directed artillery fire on the Baharestan Majles building.
THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.expl_en: Liakhov was appointed military governor of Tehran by Mohammad Ali Shah, establishing martial law and executing constitutionalist leaders.

THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.clue_en: Following the 1908 bombardment, this fiery editor of the satirical newspaper Sur-e Esrafil was strangled in the gardens of Bagh-e Shah.
THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.expl_en: Before being strangled, Jahangir Khan boldly told his executioners: 'Long live the Constitution! Our blood will nourish the tree of liberty.'

THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.clue_en: The period of reactionary monarchical rule between the bombardment of the Majles in June 1908 and the conquest of Tehran in July 1909 is called this.
THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.expl_en: The eleven-month period ended when Bakhtiari tribesmen and Tabrizi fighters stormed Tehran and deposed Mohammad Ali Shah.

THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.clue_en: During the 1908–1909 royalist siege of Tabriz, this young American missionary and teacher was shot dead leading constitutionalist fighters.
THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.expl_en: A Princeton graduate teaching at the Memorial School in Tabriz, Baskerville declared: 'I cannot stand by while these brave people fight for freedom.'

THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.clue_en: In July 1909, after constitutional forces captured Tehran, Mohammad Ali Shah fled his palace and took refuge in this foreign embassy in Zargandeh.
THE BOMBARDMENT CHRONICLES.expl_en: The Grand National Assembly formally deposed the Shah and elevated his twelve-year-old son Ahmad Shah to the throne under a regency.

MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.clue_en: In June 1952, Dr. Mohammad Mosaddegh traveled to this Dutch city to personally defend Iran's sovereign right to nationalize oil before the World Court.
MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.expl_en: The court ruled 9-to-5 that it lacked jurisdiction over the dispute, handing Mosaddegh a triumphant international legal victory over the British Empire.

MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.clue_en: During cabinet meetings and foreign diplomatic summits with Averell Harriman, Mosaddegh famously conducted high-stakes state business while wearing these clothes in bed.
MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.expl_en: Western reporters coined the term 'pajama diplomacy' as Mosaddegh exploited his genuine fainting spells and frailty to disarm hardline negotiators.

MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.clue_en: On July 21, 1952 (30 Tir 1331), nationwide mass strikes and bloody clashes in Baharestan Square forced the Shah to dismiss this short-lived British-backed Prime Minister.
MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.expl_en: Qavam held office for barely four days, issuing a radio threat to 'steer the ship of state with an iron hand' before popular fury forced his flight.

MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.ans_en: Three Years in Solitary Confinement (Followed by Village House Arrest)
MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.clue_en: Following his overthrow in August 1953, Mosaddegh was tried by a military tribunal for high treason and sentenced to this punishment.
opts_en: Three Years in Solitary Confinement (Followed by Village House Arrest)
MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.expl_en: Mosaddegh was confined under armed SAVAK guard at his private ancestral fortress in Ahmadabad-e Mosaddegh until his death on March 5, 1967.

MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.clue_en: Mosaddegh earned his doctorate in law in 1914 from this Swiss university, making him the first Iranian to earn a European doctoral degree in jurisprudence.
MOSSAD-EGH IN THE MIDDLE.expl_en: His dissertation examined Islamic wills and testamentary succession in Shi'i jurisprudence.

TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.clue_en: The rapid vocal ornamentation and melodic yodeling produced in the upper throat and falsetto characteristic of Persian classical singing is called this.
TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.expl_en: Tahrir is often compared to a nightingale's warble, requiring decades of vocal diaphragm and throat control.

TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.clue_en: Universally revered as 'Khosrow-ye Avaz-e Iran' (The Emperor of Iranian Song), this Khorasani master vocalist recorded the iconic protest anthem Morgh-e Sahar.
TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.expl_en: Shajarian was awarded the UNESCO Mozart Medal and taught generations of classical singers before his death in 2020.

TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.clue_en: Famed for singing the patriotic anthem 'Ey Iran' and wearing dark horn-rimmed glasses after losing an eye in a 1950 car crash, this singer had a velvet baritone voice.
TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.expl_en: Banan revolutionized Persian vocal style by abandoning loud shouting in favor of intimate, whispered microphone phrasing on Radio Tehran's Golha programs.

TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.clue_en: The premier cultural radio broadcast founded in 1956 by Davood Pirnia that introduced Persian classical poetry to millions of listeners was called this.
TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.expl_en: Golha produced over 1,500 episodes under categories like Golha-ye Javidan, Golha-ye Rang-a-Rang, and Yek Shakheh Gol.

TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.clue_en: This preeminent female classical vocalist, famed as 'Banu-ye Avaz-e Iran' (The Lady of Iranian Song), collaborated closely with composers Homayoun Khorram and Parviz Yahaqi.
TAHRIR-IC VOCALS.expl_en: Marzieh was the first female singer to perform on Radio Tehran's prestigious Golha-ye Rang-a-Rang programs.

CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.clue_en: Carved with the names of Mughal emperors Akbar and Jahangir before being seized by Nader Shah, this 88-carat yellow diamond was given to Tsar Nicholas I in 1829.
CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.expl_en: Prince Khosrow Mirza delivered the Shah Diamond to St. Petersburg as royal blood money to apologize for the murder of diplomat Alexander Griboyedov.

CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.clue_en: Fabricated by Paris jeweler Van Cleef & Arpels for the 1967 coronation of Empress Farah, her platinum crown featured this many carats of emeralds and diamonds.
CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.expl_en: French jeweler Pierre Arpels traveled to Tehran twenty-four times because Iranian law strictly prohibited removing the state gems from the Central Bank vault.

CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.clue_en: Discovered in Golconda, India, this massive uncut 500-carat red spinel gemstone in the Treasury is known by this historical name.
CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.expl_en: It is the largest known spinel in the world, pierced with a suspension hole originally intended for an Indian potentate's turban ornament.

CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.clue_en: The coronation mantle worn by Reza Shah in 1926 and Mohammad Reza Shah in 1967 was crafted from heavy gold brocade embroidered with this national symbol.
CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.expl_en: Woven in Isfahan workshops, the crimson velvet cape was trimmed with white ermine fur and studded with diamond rays.

CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.ans_en: The Shamshir-e Jahangosha (Conqueror of the World Sword)
CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.clue_en: This diamond-studded gold scabbard and curved shamshir saber in the Treasury, carried by Nader Shah at the Battle of Karnal, was known as this.
opts_en: The Shamshir-e Jahangosha (Conqueror of the World Sword)
CROWN JEWELS AND CROWD JEERS.expl_en: The hilt is encrusted with over 1,700 diamonds, engraved with Persian verses celebrating Nader's military dominion over India and Central Asia.

JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.clue_en: The radical pro-Bolshevik member of the Jangali leadership who ousted Mirza Kuchik Khan in August 1920 to proclaim a full Marxist republic was named this.
JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.expl_en: Ehsanollah Khan marched a ragtag Red Army toward Tehran, but was routed at Pol-e Rudbar by Reza Khan's Cossacks; he fled to Baku where Stalin purged him in 1939.

JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.ans_en: The Committee of Islamic Unity (Ettehad-e Eslam)
JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.clue_en: The secret society formed by Mirza Kuchik Khan and his companions in Tehran in 1914 before taking up arms in the Caspian forests was known as this.
opts_en: The Committee of Islamic Unity (Ettehad-e Eslam)
JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.expl_en: The committee sought to expel British and Russian occupation troops while resisting the corrupt central government in Tehran.

JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.clue_en: The British expeditionary force dispatched through western Iran to the Caspian Sea in 1918 to seize the Baku oil fields was nicknamed this after its general.
JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.expl_en: Dunsterville fought pitched battles against the Jangalis at the Manjil bridge before reaching Anzali and sailing to Baku.

JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.clue_en: The official newspaper published in the forests of Gilan by the Jangali Movement, printed on a portable lithograph press, was named this.
JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.expl_en: Edited by Hosein Kasma'i, Jangal proclaimed its motto: 'Iran belongs to Iranians; foreigners must leave.'

JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.clue_en: The treaty signed on February 26, 1921 between Moscow and Tehran that renounced all Tsarist concessions and caused the Red Army to abandon the Jangalis was this.
JUNGLE GUERRILLAS OF GILAN.expl_en: Article 6 granted Soviet troops the right to enter Iran if a third power used Iranian territory to threaten Russia, a clause Moscow cited during WWI in 1941.

THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.clue_en: Completed in 1970, this 1,100-kilometer natural gas pipeline transported southern Khuzestan gas across the Alborz to Astara on the Soviet border.
THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.expl_en: In exchange for natural gas, the Soviet Union financed and constructed the Aryamehr (Isfahan) Steel Mill and the Arak heavy machine plant.

THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.clue_en: Built near Behbahan in Khuzestan to process gas for the Soviet IGAT pipeline, this facility was the largest natural gas refinery in the Middle East.
THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.expl_en: Bid Boland treated one billion cubic feet of gas per day, extracting natural gas liquids before piping dry gas across the Zagros Mountains.

THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.clue_en: The shared offshore natural gas field beneath the Persian Gulf, the largest in the world, is known as North Dome in Qatar and this in Iran.
THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.expl_en: Holding an estimated 51 trillion cubic meters of gas, South Pars accounts for over sixty percent of Iran's domestic gas consumption.

THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.ans_en: Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea
THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.clue_en: Signed in Aktau, Kazakhstan in August 2018, this landmark convention settled the legal status of the Caspian Sea among its five littoral states.
opts_en: Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea
THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.expl_en: The convention forbade non-littoral military forces from entering the Caspian, while leaving the final delimitation of the seabed open to bilateral negotiations.

THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.clue_en: The state enterprise founded in 1965 to develop domestic urban gas grids and cross-country transport pipelines is known by this acronym.
THE CASPIAN PIPELINE DREAM.expl_en: NIGC expanded Iran's domestic piped natural gas network to cover over 95% of Iranian households, one of the most extensive urban gas grids on earth.

A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.clue_en: The Shah's 1951 wedding to Queen Soraya Esfandiari Bakhtiari featured a custom gown crafted by Christian Dior adorned with 20,000 feathers and this many diamonds.
A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.expl_en: The gown weighed over twenty kilograms; the Shah reportedly asked an officer to cut off eight meters of the velvet train with a razor during the reception to ease her burden.

A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.clue_en: Queen Soraya was the daughter of Khalil Esfandiari Bakhtiari, a prominent chieftain of this powerful southwestern nomadic confederation.
A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.expl_en: Her mother Eva Karl was German; the marriage was designed to cement an alliance between the Pahlavi dynasty and the powerful Bakhtiari tribal nobility.

A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.ans_en: Three Faces of a Woman (I tre volti)
A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.clue_en: Following her divorce in 1958, Queen Soraya launched a brief acting career in Europe, starring in the 1965 Italian anthology film titled this.
opts_en: Three Faces of a Woman (I tre volti)
A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.expl_en: Directed by Michelangelo Antonioni and Franco Indovina, the Shah reportedly purchased and destroyed all prints of the film circulating in Iran.

A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.clue_en: Princess Fawzia of Egypt, the Shah's first wife, divorced him in 1948 and returned to Cairo, later marrying this Egyptian colonel and diplomat.
A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.expl_en: Fawzia lived quietly in Alexandria after the Egyptian monarchy was abolished, passing away in 2013 at the age of 91.

A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.clue_en: To secure imperial succession in 1959, the Shah married 21-year-old architecture student Farah Diba, whom he met at this embassy in Paris.
A MARRIAGE OF INCONVENIENCE.expl_en: Ambassador Ardeshir Zahedi and his wife Princess Shahnaz introduced Farah to the Shah, recommending her as an ideal modern, cultured Iranian empress.

THE RED AND THE BLACK.ans_en: The Alliance of the Red and the Black
THE RED AND THE BLACK.clue_en: The Shah frequently used this derogatory phrase to describe the tactical alliance between Marxist leftists and religious clerical reactionaries.
opts_en: The Alliance of the Red and the Black
THE RED AND THE BLACK.expl_en: The Shah argued that communists (Red) and Islamic fundamentalists (Black) were united in destroying Pahlavi modernization and dragging Iran into darkness.

THE RED AND THE BLACK.clue_en: The influential Marxist-Leninist pro-Soviet party founded in 1941 by veteran communists released from Reza Shah's prisons was named this.
THE RED AND THE BLACK.expl_en: The Tudeh Party built the largest labor unions and intellectual networks in Iranian history before being banned following the 1949 assassination attempt on the Shah.

THE RED AND THE BLACK.clue_en: This charismatic sociologist synthesized Shi'i martyrdom theology with Marxist revolutionary theory, inspiring thousands of young student militants.
THE RED AND THE BLACK.expl_en: Lecturing at Hosseiniyeh Ershad, Shariati coined the concept of 'Red Shi'ism' (revolutionary martyrdom of Imam Hussein) versus 'Black Shi'ism' (mourning submission under the Safavids).

THE RED AND THE BLACK.clue_en: In February 1971, thirteen armed Marxist guerrillas attacked a gendarmerie post in this Gilan village, launching the modern armed guerrilla movement in Iran.
THE RED AND THE BLACK.expl_en: The assault gave birth to the Organization of Iranian People's Fada'i Guerrillas (OIPFG), immortalized in Ahmad Shamlou's poetry.

THE RED AND THE BLACK.ans_en: Confess to Espionage for the Soviet Union (Televised Confessions)
THE RED AND THE BLACK.clue_en: In May 1983, the leaders of the Tudeh Party, including First Secretary Nurredin Kianouri, appeared on state television to do this.
opts_en: Confess to Espionage for the Soviet Union (Televised Confessions)
Announce the dissolution of the party
THE RED AND THE BLACK.expl_en: Kianouri and eighty veteran communist leaders confessed to sending Iranian state secrets to the KGB, ending forty years of organized communist activity in Iran.

AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.clue_en: The top-scoring F-14 Tomcat fighter ace in aviation history, credited with 11 confirmed air-to-air kills during the Iran-Iraq War, was this pilot.
AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.expl_en: Flying Tomcat tail number 3-6079, Zandi downed eight Iraqi MiGs and three Sukhois, surviving being shot down by an Iraqi Mirage F1 in 1988.

AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.clue_en: Carried exclusively by the Iranian Air Force's F-14 Tomcats, this 1,000-pound long-range radar-guided missile could destroy enemy jets up to 100 miles away.
AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.expl_en: Iranian technicians developed domestic battery cooling packs and reverse-engineered parts to keep the Phoenix operational throughout the eight-year war.

AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.clue_en: On September 23, 1980, hours after Iraq's invasion, Iran launched this massive 140-aircraft airstrike targeting every major Iraqi military airbase.
AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.expl_en: Named after Arash the Archer's mythic bow, Kaman 99 crippled Iraqi runways and destroyed dozens of planes on the ground.

AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.clue_en: During the 1988 'War of the Cities', Saddam Hussein bombarded residential neighborhoods in Tehran with modified long-range Soviet missiles called this.
AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.expl_en: Iraq extended the range of standard Soviet Scuds by welding three missile airframes together and reducing the warhead weight, striking deep into Tehran.

AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.clue_en: On July 3, 1988, this guided missile cruiser of the US Navy shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Persian Gulf, killing all 290 civilians aboard.
AIRLINES AND AIR RAIDS.expl_en: The cruiser mistook the climbing civilian Airbus A300 for an attacking F-14 Tomcat, firing two surface-to-air missiles while inside Iranian territorial waters.

MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.clue_en: Considered the Raphael of the East, this 15th-century Herat master miniaturist revolutionized Persian painting with naturalistic human poses and vibrant architectural settings.
MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.expl_en: Behzad directed the royal ateliers of both Timurid Sultan Husayn Bayqara in Herat and Safavid Shah Ismail I in Tabriz.

MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.clue_en: Leading the Isfahan School under Shah Abbas I, this painter abandoned grand royal epics to pioneer intimate, single-sheet portraits of calligraphers, lovers, and dervishes.
MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.expl_en: Reza Abbasi was awarded the prestigious royal honorific 'Abbasi' by Shah Abbas for his fluid, expressive calligraphic brushwork.

MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.clue_en: Created in Tabriz in the 1530s with 258 exquisite miniature paintings, this monumental illuminated royal manuscript was dismembered and sold at auction in the 20th century.
MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.expl_en: In 1994, the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art successfully traded Willem de Kooning's painting Woman III for 118 dispersed folios of the Tahmasp Shahnameh.

MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.clue_en: To achieve luminous, permanent colors, Persian miniaturists ground precious lapis lazuli from Badakhshan into powder to produce this rich deep blue pigment.
MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.expl_en: Lapis pigment was mixed with egg white and gum arabic, retaining its dazzling celestial brilliance for over five centuries without fading.

MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.clue_en: Fine single-hair brushes used by master miniaturists for microscopic facial features and beard hairs were crafted from the hair of this animal.
MINIATURE GOLF NO MINIATURE ART.expl_en: Hairs were plucked from the tails of Caucasian squirrels, bound into bird quill shafts to form an ultra-sharp point.

THE ANJOMAN GANG.clue_en: Formed in 1906, this provincial constitutional council in Tabriz wielded executive power, collecting taxes and directing street barricades against royalist troops.
THE ANJOMAN GANG.expl_en: The Tabriz Anjoman operated as a parallel revolutionary government, demanding strict accountability from MPs and publishing its own daily gazette.

THE ANJOMAN GANG.clue_en: Underground secret bulletins criticizing royal despotism and distributed under cover of darkness during the Constitutional Revolution were known as this.
THE ANJOMAN GANG.expl_en: Pasted onto mosque walls and slipped under merchant doors at night, Shabnamehs exposed court corruption and galvanized street demonstrations.

THE ANJOMAN GANG.ans_en: Anjoman-e Mokhadderat-e Vatan (Society of Patriotic Women)
THE ANJOMAN GANG.clue_en: The pioneering women's secret constitutional society founded in Tehran in 1910 to establish modern girls' schools and boycott foreign textiles was called this.
opts_en: Anjoman-e Mokhadderat-e Vatan (Society of Patriotic Women)
THE ANJOMAN GANG.expl_en: Members like Agha Begum and Sedigheh Dowlatabadi confronted MPs at gunpoint in 1911, warning them not to surrender to Russian ultimatums.

THE ANJOMAN GANG.clue_en: The social democratic party founded in Baku in 1904 that sent armed volunteer fighters and bombs to defend constitutionalists in Tabriz was known as this.
THE ANJOMAN GANG.expl_en: Headed by Nariman Narimanov in Baku, it established secret cells across northern Iran and organized the Caucasian volunteer brigades (Mujahideen).

THE ANJOMAN GANG.clue_en: The secret society formed in Tehran in 1904 by Mirza Jahangir Khan and Nazem al-Islam Kermani that met in secret to plot the constitutional movement was called this.
THE ANJOMAN GANG.expl_en: Members took oaths on the Quran in darkened rooms behind black curtains to maintain total anonymity while planning the merchant strikes.

TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.clue_en: On April 24, 1980, the United States launched this secret joint military operation to rescue 52 American hostages held in Tehran.
TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.expl_en: The operation collapsed at a remote staging site in the Dasht-e Kavir desert near Tabas following hydraulic failures and a catastrophic collision.

TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.clue_en: The secret desert airstrip and helicopter refueling rendezvous point located 200 miles southeast of Tehran was codenamed this.
TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.expl_en: Six C-130 Hercules transport planes and eight RH-53D Sea Stallion helicopters rendezvoused on a remote salt bed crossed by the Yazd-Tabas highway.

TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.clue_en: The elite US Army special operations unit that formed the primary hostage rescue assault force during Operation Eagle Claw was this.
TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.expl_en: Founded in 1977 by Colonel Charlie Beckwith, Eagle Claw was Delta Force's very first operational combat deployment.

TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.clue_en: During the abortive withdrawal at Desert One, an RH-53D helicopter collided in a giant fireball with this type of aircraft.
TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.expl_en: The collision killed eight American servicemen—five airmen and three Marines—destroying both aircraft and triggering an immediate evacuation.

TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.clue_en: The dense, blinding suspended desert dust storms encountered by the helicopters flying low over the Dasht-e Kavir are known by this Arabic meteorological term.
TABAS SANDS AND HELICOPTER COMMANDS.expl_en: Two helicopters suffered generator and gyro failures inside the haboob, forcing one to turn back to the carrier USS Nimitz.

THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.clue_en: Constructed between 1302 and 1312 in Zanjan province, this UNESCO-listed monument features the third largest brick dome in the world after Florence and Hagia Sophia.
THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.expl_en: Rising 48 meters high with a double-shell brick dome covered in turquoise glazed faience, it weighs over 200 tons.

THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.clue_en: The Mongol Ilkhanid monarch who built Soltaniyeh and converted to Twelver Shi'ism, taking the regnal title Mohammad Khodabandeh, was named this.
THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.expl_en: Born a Christian and baptized Nicholas, Oljeitu studied Buddhism and Sunni jurisprudence before converting to Shi'ism under Allamah al-Hilli.

THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.clue_en: Oljeitu originally constructed the magnificent mausoleum at Soltaniyeh with the intention of exhuming and re-interring the sacred remains of these two Shi'i Imams.
THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.expl_en: When the clerics of Najaf and Karbala vehemently refused to surrender the bodies, Oljeitu consecrated the monument as his own imperial tomb.

THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.ans_en: Double-Shell Hollow Brick Dome (Two concentric shells)
THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.clue_en: Soltaniyeh's innovative architectural design, which directly influenced Brunelleschi's dome for the Florence Cathedral, relies on this engineering feature.
opts_en: Double-Shell Hollow Brick Dome (Two concentric shells)
THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.expl_en: The hollow space between the inner ceiling and outer turquoise dome reduced the dead weight load on the supporting octagonal walls by fifty percent.

THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.clue_en: Surrounding the base of the Soltaniyeh dome, this number of slender decorative turquoise minarets were erected atop the eight corners of the building.
THE SULTAN OF SOLTANIYEH.expl_en: The eight minarets acted as structural counterweights and vertical wind-breakers, protecting the brick dome from gale-force plateau winds.

THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.ans_en: Ali-Qoli Khan Sardar As'ad (Sardar As'ad II)
THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.clue_en: The cultured Bakhtiari Ilkhan who had traveled widely in Paris and led the tribal cavalry that stormed Tehran in July 1909 was named this.
opts_en: Ali-Qoli Khan Sardar As'ad (Sardar As'ad II)
THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.expl_en: Sardar As'ad financed the march using Bakhtiari oil royalties, forming an unbreakable military alliance with Yeprem Khan's northern fighters.

THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.clue_en: In January 1909, Bakhtiari horsemen led by Zargham al-Saltaneh captured this grand Safavid capital, expelling the royalist governor.
THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.expl_en: The capture of Isfahan broke Mohammad Ali Shah's strategic rear, inspiring tribes across the Zagros to declare for the Constitution.

THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.clue_en: Under the 1905 agreement with William Knox D'Arcy, the Bakhtiari khans received this annual percentage of dividends and protection subsidies.
THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.expl_en: This private pipeline protection treaty made the Bakhtiari khans immensely wealthy and financially autonomous from the central government in Tehran.

THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.clue_en: The traditional semi-annual nomadic migration of the Bakhtiari tribes between winter lowland pastures (Garamsir) and summer alpine meadows is known as this.
THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.expl_en: Immortalized in Merian C. Cooper's 1925 documentary film Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life, 50,000 tribesmen and 500,000 animals swam the freezing Karun River.

THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.clue_en: The sleeveless black-and-white striped felt tunic worn proudly by Bakhtiari men into battle and during seasonal migration is called this.
THE BAKHTIARI MARCH.expl_en: Woven by Bakhtiari women from sheep's wool, its geometric pattern is said to symbolize the ancient stepped battlements of Chogha Zanbil.

RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.ans_en: Crown Prince Mohammad Reza (Later Mohammad Reza Shah)
RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.clue_en: On April 24, 1940, Radio Tehran was officially inaugurated with a live speech delivered from the wireless transmission mast at Pahlavi Wireless by this monarch.
opts_en: Crown Prince Mohammad Reza (Later Mohammad Reza Shah)
RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.expl_en: Broadcasting with a 20-kilowatt transmitter built by Germany's Telefunken, Radio Tehran was initially limited to five hours of evening broadcasts per day.

RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.clue_en: During WWII, Nazi Germany broadcast Persian propaganda across Iran featuring this antisemitic Persian announcer known as 'Bahram the Persian'.
RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.expl_en: Broadcasting nightly from Radio Berlin, Shahrokh claimed Hitler was the promised Twelfth Imam, urging Iranians to sabotage Allied railway supply lines.

RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.ans_en: Homa Zahedi (or Moluk Zarabi / Subversive Broadcaster)
RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.clue_en: On the afternoon of August 19, 1953, royalist army officers seized Radio Tehran, where this actress famously shouted into the microphone: 'The traitor Mosaddegh has fled!'
opts_en: Homa Zahedi (or Moluk Zarabi / Subversive Broadcaster)
RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.expl_en: Royalist conspirators broadcast martial music and martial law edicts from the wireless studios while tanks encircled Mosaddegh's private house on Kakh Street.

RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.clue_en: In the 1970s, the clandestine National Voice of Iran (Sedaye Melli-ye Iran) beamed anti-Shah communist propaganda into Tehran from this Soviet republic capital.
RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.expl_en: Funded by the KGB and staffed by exiled Tudeh activists, it instructed Iranian factory workers and oil technicians on how to organize illegal general strikes.

RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.clue_en: The iconic four-tone chimes played on Radio Tehran to announce the top-of-the-hour news broadcast were composed on this traditional Persian percussion instrument.
RADIO TEHRAN CALLING.expl_en: Struck with felt-tipped wooden mallets (Mezrab), the shimmering acoustic chimes became the instantly recognizable auditory trademark of National Iranian Radio.

THE LION OF AZERBAIJAN.clue_en: Wounded during the Park-e Atabak disarmament showdown in Tehran in 1910, this constitutional folk hero of Tabriz died four years later, buried in Shah Abdol-Azim.
THE LION OF AZERBAIJAN.expl_en: Sattar Khan took refuge with his horsemen in Park-e Atabak; government forces under Yeprem Khan opened fire to enforce disarmament, crippling Sattar Khan with a bullet to his ankle.

THE LION OF AZERBAIJAN.ans_en: The Banner of Iran (The Iranian Flag)
THE LION OF AZERBAIJAN.clue_en: During the eleven-month siege of Tabriz in 1908, when foreign diplomats urged him to surrender and raise the Russian flag over his house, Sattar Khan declared: 'I want seven states to take shelter under...'
opts_en: The Banner of Iran (The Iranian Flag)
THE LION OF AZERBAIJAN.expl_en: Sattar Khan boldly retorted: 'I want seven foreign empires to submit under the shadow of the Iranian flag; shall I then surrender under a foreign banner?'

THE POISONED CHALICE LETTER.ans_en: Drinking a Chalice of Poison (Jām-e Zahr)
THE POISONED CHALICE LETTER.clue_en: In his broadcast letter of July 20, 1988 accepting UN Resolution 598 to end the Iran-Iraq War, Ayatollah Khomeini famously stated that doing so was more deadly than this.
opts_en: Drinking a Chalice of Poison (Jām-e Zahr)
THE POISONED CHALICE LETTER.expl_en: Khomeini wrote: 'Happy are those who were martyred in battle; woe to me that I survived to drink the poisoned chalice of accepting this resolution.'

THE POISONED CHALICE LETTER.clue_en: The United Nations Security Council resolution passed in July 1987 that established the formal diplomatic framework for ending the Iran-Iraq War was this number.
THE POISONED CHALICE LETTER.expl_en: Resolution 598 called for an immediate ceasefire, withdrawal to international borders, exchange of all POWs, and an impartial tribunal to identify the aggressor.

THE GALA OF PEACOCKS.clue_en: The historic Paris fashion house commissioned to design the blue-and-gold imperial staff and hostess uniforms for the 1971 Persepolis Celebrations was this.
THE GALA OF PEACOCKS.expl_en: Lanvin designed hundreds of tailored uniforms with gold braided epaulettes for palace staff, waiters, and drivers serving the world's royalty in the tent city.

THE GALA OF PEACOCKS.clue_en: The exclusive French caterer flown into Persepolis with 165 chefs, sommeliers, and waiters to prepare the five-course banquets for the 1971 gala was this.
THE GALA OF PEACOCKS.expl_en: Maxim's shut down its flagship Rue Royale restaurant in Paris for two weeks, flying eighteen tons of food and rare French wines into Shiraz on military transports.

THE FORGOTTEN CAPITAL.clue_en: In 1555, Shah Tahmasp I moved the Safavid capital from Tabriz to this strategic inland plateau city to protect the court from Ottoman border cannon fire.
THE FORGOTTEN CAPITAL.expl_en: Qazvin served as the imperial capital for 43 years, where Tahmasp laid out the first Chahar Bagh royal boulevard and Ali Qapu portal gate.

THE FORGOTTEN CAPITAL.ans_en: Chehel Sotoun of Qazvin (Kakh-e Chehel Sotoun)
THE FORGOTTEN CAPITAL.clue_en: The surviving royal palace pavilion of Shah Tahmasp I in Qazvin, known for its two-story wooden octagonal columned porches, is called this.
opts_en: Chehel Sotoun of Qazvin (Kakh-e Chehel Sotoun)
THE FORGOTTEN CAPITAL.expl_en: Constructed in 1550, its wall frescoes depict Tahmasp's reception of Mughal Emperor Humayun seeking military refuge in Iran.

THE GOLDEN VEST OF REZA SHAH.ans_en: A Heavy Silver/Gold Pocket Watch (Silver Watch in his Vest Pocket)
THE GOLDEN VEST OF REZA SHAH.clue_en: In 1915, during WWI fighting against pro-German rebel tribes in Hamadan, Cossack Colonel Reza Khan was struck in the chest by a bullet stopped by this object.
opts_en: A Heavy Silver/Gold Pocket Watch (Silver Watch in his Vest Pocket)
A Quran in his breast pocket
THE GOLDEN VEST OF REZA SHAH.expl_en: The dented Russian silver watch absorbed the kinetic energy of the bullet, leaving him with a massive purple bruise but saving his life.

THE GOLDEN VEST OF REZA SHAH.clue_en: The rapid-firing heavy machine gun that Reza Khan operated with deadly skill during his early Cossack military career, earning him the nickname 'Reza Maxim', was this.
THE GOLDEN VEST OF REZA SHAH.expl_en: His unmatched proficiency in disassembling, clearing jams, and laying down suppressive fire with the Maxim gun earned him the rank of officer and the legendary military moniker 'Reza Maxim'.
